QUEEN'S PRINTER AND CONTROLLER OF STATIONERY OTTAWA, 1963 HOUSE OF COMMONS

speechtext: Monday, September 30, 1963

maintopic: STATEMENT BY MR. SPEAKER RESPECTING SEATING ARRANGEMENTS
STATEMENT BY MR. SPEAKER RESPECTING SEATING ARRANGEMENTS
speechtext:
May I take this first opportunity to welcome all hon. members back to the house to what I am sure will be a very energetic, strenuous and without doubt profitable session for the public of Canada.

It gives me pleasure to find us all together again, ready to get back to work.
I am quite convinced that the months to come will be of benefit to all our fellow-Canadians thanks to the knowledge and intelligence of all those around me, both on my right and on my left.
Now I have a statement to make, and I thought of expressing myself both in English and in French. On the other hand, it might be better if the French text were distributed immediately so that hon. members who wish to do so can refer to it while I read the English.

Before calling the orders of the day I would crave the indulgence of hon. members in order to permit me to make a statement on a situation which has developed since the adjournment of the house on August 2. The problem with which the house is faced is a new one. May I be allowed to refer, in a chronological order, to certain correspondence by which I was apprised of the facts.
On September 9, 1963, the hon. member for Lapointe wrote me a letter to the effect that his party had chosen a new leader and claiming certain rights and privileges.
On September 13, 1963, the hon. member for Red Deer wrote me a letter to the effect "that the separation of Mr. Real Caouette and his followers from the party poses several problems".
On September 16 the hon. member for Villeneuve wrote me a letter reading in part as follows:

Since September 1, our movement has become a national group under the name of Ralliement Creditistes.

On September 18 the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre wrote me a letter reading in part:
In view of recent developments it seems quite clear that the New Democratic party, with its 17 members, is now the third largest group in the House of Commons.
Later on in the letter he adds:
Since we are now the largest of the smaller parties we will expect to be seated immediately next to the official opposition.
The events which have taken place and the correspondence in relation thereto, which X am prepared to lay on the table if the house so desires, have given rise to a number of questions. Among them is first the recognition of a new party and of its leader; second, the seating arrangements in the chamber; then the question of the allowance to "the leader of a party that has a recognized membership of 12 or more persons in the House of Commons"; and following that the allocation of rooms, personnel, and other matters. I do not think it is necessary to deal with those problems at the moment; it is sufficient to mention them.
"Party" as defined by Burke in the classical passage on the subject, "Thoughts on the Causes of the Present Discontent" is a body of men united for promoting the national interest on some particular principle in which they are all agreed.
Have we a new party according to this definition and, if so, has this party been recognized by the house? To my mind this is a question for the house to decide.
The question of third parties in itself is not a new one. After the last election, apart from the Liberal and Conservative parties, as all hon. members know, there were recognized the Social Credit party and the New Democratic party.
Third parties have existed continually in the house practically since 1921. In 1921 there were 117 Liberals, 50 Conservatives, 66 Progressives and 2 other members, independent and labour. This third party situation has continued throughout the years, that is after the elections of 1925, 1926, 1930, 1935, 1940, 1945, 1949, 1953, 1957, 1958, 1962 and 1963.
If the house is used to third parties, that is to having a third and fourth party in the house, it will be admitted that it creates quite a new situation to have a third party divide

Seating Arrangements in Chamber into two sections or blocks a few months after a general election and during an adjournment of the house.
I have already indicated some of the problems which are created by this unprecedented situation. There now remains to consider my position as Speaker of the house in connection with these recent events.
The legal rights and duties of the Speaker are to be found in the statutes of Canada, the standing orders of the house, in the constitutional and parliamentary authors and finally in the customs and precedents which have become constitutional conventions. According to Campion, the Speaker is the representative of the house itself, in its powers, proceedings and dignity, and the chief characteristics attaching to the office of Speaker of the House of Commons are authority and impartiality. Campion states also that it is the duty of the Speaker to see that the house is properly constituted before it proceeds to business.
It is in consequence among the duties of the Speaker to see that the standing orders of the house are followed in the course of its procedures and that the privileges of the house, once they have been defined and recognized, are protected. It is also the duty of the Speaker to be impartial and removed from politics, which has always been my aim since, hon. members, you did me the honour to elect me as your Speaker.
Sir Erskine May, sixteenth edition, page 42, has stated:
that parliamentary privilege is the sum of peculiar rights enjoyed by each house collectively as a constituent part of the high court of parliament, and by members of each house individually, without which they could not discharge their functions, and which exceed those possessed by other bodies or individuals. Thus privilege, though part of the law of the land, is to a certain extent an exception from the ordinary law.
Dawson, in his book on "The Government of Canada", writes:
The privileges, immunities and powers of the house of parliament of Canada are thus potentially those of the British House of Commons, although their primary basis is statutory and not established custom and inherent right.
In the Canadian house, questions of privilege take a wide range, but it may be stated in general terms that they refer to all matters affecting the rights and immunities of the house collectively, the rights of recognized parties, or to the position and conduct of members in their representative character. In this category may be placed questions affecting the recognition of a party, touching the seat or election of members, questions affecting the internal economy or proceedings of the house.
If the Speaker is to take any notice of these privileges and at the same time to
[Mr. Speaker.!
exercise the high degree of independence and impartiality which is justly expected of him, it is well that those privileges be first defined and decided by the house itself. Anson, in "Law and Custom of the Constitution", at page 130, as quoted by Beauchesne, fourth edition, page 94, says:
The house has always asserted the right to provide for the constitution of its own body, the right to regulate its own proceedings and the right to enforce its privileges.
Allow me to refer once more to the special traditions that surround the office of Speaker. While he is the servant of the house he is, at the same time, its spokesman and its symbol. His value to the house and its members continues effectively only when the house assists him in every way to maintain his dignity and his impartiality, and during my short term I have had the confidence of the house to the point where I know I can place myself and my problems in its hands.
It seems to me that having in mind the authorities from Sir Erskine May to Lord Campion, from Bourinot to Beauchesne and from Anson to McGregor Dawson and many others, a situation such as that now facing the house must be resolved by the house itself. It is not one where the Speaker ought by himself to take a position where any group of members might feel that their interests as a group or a party have been prejudiced. Nor should the Speaker be put in the position where he must decide, to the advantage or to the disadvantage of any group or party, matters affecting the character or existence of a party, for this surely would signify that the Speaker had taken what was almost a political decision, a decision where the question involves the rights and privileges of the house itself.
I cannot conclude this statement without some reference to the significance of these events for the future of the definition and status of parties in this house. It is not my place to evaluate the significance of these matters for the future of the ever changing structure and character of political parties; yet it is my duty, I believe, to bring to the attention of the house the novel character of the situation now before it, and more particularly the payment of allowances and the effect on the organization of parliament and parties and of the work of this house that naturally must be reflected by the emergence from time to time of new groups that invite the house to accord them the status of parties. Profound constitutional questions arise; for example, can a group of members which did not exist as a party at the time

of the election of a parliament be recognized as a party before it has submitted itself to the electorate?
Having indicated this new development to the house with its suggestive consequences, may I end my statement by relying upon the house to give me the necessary guidance required for the due administration of my duties in view of the issues presented to me by the letters from the hon. members concerned, and which have required me to make this statement today.
For these reasons I am of the opinion that the interests of the house, of members and of all parties will best be served if the questions raised by the hon. members for Lapointe, Red Deer, Villeneuve and Winnipeg North Centre in the various letters addressed to me were referred at this time to the proper committee for consideration and report so as to bring about a solution thereto.
As Speaker, I shall carry out the orders of the house and apply such interpretations to the rules of the house as the house itself may require of me.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
maintopic: STATEMENT BY MR. SPEAKER RESPECTING SEATING ARRANGEMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if I may I should like to rise on a question of privilege. My point of privilege relates to an aspect of the matter covered by the statement you have just made to the house. I think I should say at this time that I believe the house will agree with me that we are all indebted to you for the very helpful statement you have made with respect to the situation which now confronts us in this House of Commons. I may say also that at the conclusion of my remarks I should like to indicate my agreement with the suggestion you have made; in fact, as a matter of privilege I will suggest a motion along the very lines of your statement.
First of all may I indicate why in my view I feel, on behalf of this group, the New Democratic party, that there is a question of privilege to be raised at this time. Following the election of June 18, 1962, when the Social Credit party and the New Democratic party both came to this house with certain numbers of members, the question of our seating and our priority arose in discussions between representatives of these parties and the then Speaker, Mr. Michener, and the subsequent Speaker, the present hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert). It was my contention that on the basis of the precedents of former years, notably 1935 and 1940, seniority and certain other considerations entitled us in the New Democratic party to be recognized as the third party in the house. May I make it clear that we in this party accepted the judgment that was given by Mr. Speaker
Seating Arrangements in Chamber Michener and by Mr. Speaker Lambert that other considerations had to be set aside in light of one overriding consideration, namely the number of members in each group. Therefore, because following the election of June 18, 1962, the Social Credit party had 30 members and we had only 19, the Social Credit party was recognized as third party in the house and we were given the position of fourth party in the house.
A few months later came the election of April 8, 1963. As a result of that election again the Social Credit party had more members than we had: they had 24 on the night of the election, which was reduced to 23 a little later. In any case our number, as hon. members know, was 17. The issue was raised again but there was no extended argument about it, because we were all agreed that the decision had been made the year before, namely that so far as the seating of, and other matters affecting, small parties were concerned the number of members was the key factor. The Social Credit party had more members than the New Democratic party had; therefore the Social Credit party was given third place.
Mr. Speaker, as you have indicated in your statement, I wrote you about this matter on behalf of this party on September 18, pointing out to you that reports in the press seemed to make it quite clear that we, with our 17 members, had become the third largest party in the house. In my letter, which I note you are prepared to table-I should be glad if all this correspondence were tabled-I did not happen to name the Social Credit party, but I referred to recent events and said that in the light of these events we were obviously the third party in size in this house, and I indicated that I expected that when the house met on September 30 we would be seated in third position next to the official opposition.
I might point out, Mr. Speaker, that on the two previous occasions to which I have referred-the occasions following the election of 1962 and following the election of 1963- the decision was made before the house met. When the house met we sat in the seats allotted to us. Therefore it was my view when I wrote my letter of September 18 that this decision should have been made before today, and that on coming into the house today we should have been placed in seats which would recognize our position as the third largest party in the house.
There is involved, so far as our position is concerned, not only the question of where we sit; because after all it is a privilege to sit anywhere in this house, whether in the front row or the back row, up at that end or down at this end; there is a question of the

Seating Arrangements in Chamber order of speakers in debates, the question of the right to move amendments in certain cases, and so on. Therefore we feel it is a matter of concern not only to us but to all members of the house, a matter of concern to all who want the practices and privileges of the house to be respected, that our position, if we are the third party in size in the house, should be that of the third party as far as seating position and other matters are concerned.
As I say, it was my belief and contention that this decision should have been made before we took our places in the house today, and that we should have been given our seats next to the official opposition. However, I recognize readily that to have made such a move earlier than today would have involved other considerations. It would have involved the questions you have raised, Mr. Speaker, as to whether there has in fact been a division of the Social Credit party into two parties, whether they are two parts of the same party or two separate parties, and so on. From what we have read in the papers I find it strange they should be sitting together, cheek by jowl, without exchanging any blows; at least not yet.

maintopic: STATEMENT BY MR. SPEAKER RESPECTING SEATING ARRANGEMENTS
speechtext: No worse than sitting beside you.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
maintopic: STATEMENT BY MR. SPEAKER RESPECTING SEATING ARRANGEMENTS
speechtext:
May I indulge in the use of at least one French word I know, and say "touche".
There is also the question of determining, if we are to be moved up, the order in which the other two parties are to sit. I realize it is unfair to ask you, Mr. Speaker, to make this decision in advance. I think the situation is sufficiently unusual that your suggestion is an appropriate one, namely that this is a matter which should be decided by the house. For these reasons we are prepared to possess our souls in patience for a few days so far as seating is concerned. We are prepared to see this matter referred to a special committee of the house so that the committee may consider it and bring back its findings at the earliest possible date. We do think that if it is established before that date-and one has to get the evidence in order to find out-that there are now three so-called smaller parties and that their numbers are 17, 13 and 11, there should be no question but that the party with 17 should be the third party in the house and sit next to the official opposition. We think that if the committee could ascertain the facts and make a decision quickly in this respect it should do so, and that the change should be made. If it takes longer to decide as between the other two, perhaps the committee would take somewhat longer to determine that particular issue.
I think the house is indebted to Your Honour for having taken the trouble to prepare the statement you have given us today. It is a statement that is likely to be referred to a number of times in the course of the progress of this parliament. One does not know what lies ahead in terms of our parliamentary arrangements. The people of Canada have the right to elect the governments and parties they wish to elect. Nevertheless, here in this house it is our responsibility to see that the arrangements we make with regard to the seating of parties, the priority of speakers, the moving of amendments and so on are made in accordance with the best practices of parliamentary democracy.
Therefore it gives me pleasure to move a motion along the lines suggested in the latter part of Your Honour's statement. I move, seconded by my hon. friend from Burnaby-Coquitlam:
That the matters raised and the statement made to the house this day by Mr. Speaker be referred to the committee on privileges and elections and that the said committee be instructed to report its findings thereon to the house with all convenient speed.

speakeroldname: Righi Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: STATEMENT BY MR. SPEAKER RESPECTING SEATING ARRANGEMENTS
speechtext:
First may I say that I think Your Honour has done the house a great deal of benefit by the research which has been shown in the production of this statement you have just made. I was particularly interested in the quotation you made from Burke, the title of his speech being "Thoughts on the Causes of the Present Discontent". It was very applicable and it was an example, once again, of history reliving itself, though in a manner not within the contemplation of Burke at the time he made the speech in question.
The responsibility which will rest on this committee will be a great one; to determine when is a party not a party; when does disagreement within a party cause such a cleavage as to proliferate the number of parties within a party.

maintopic: STATEMENT BY MR. SPEAKER RESPECTING SEATING ARRANGEMENTS
speechtext: It might happen to you.

maintopic: STATEMENT BY MR. SPEAKER RESPECTING SEATING ARRANGEMENTS
speechtext:
I might say also, to my friends on the left, the question might arise as to whether the New Democratic party is a separate party or whether it is just a section of the Liberal party ready to vote with the government on occasions or to abstain altogether. These are all questions which will, I am sure, be of tremendous interest as this committee carries out the responsibility which will belong to it should the house pass the motion before us.
However, I must say that all of this, all these events, underline and emphasize the danger I pointed out when I spoke in the

house last July on the measure which provided for the payment of $4,000 per year to leaders of parties other than the official opposition. If such a payment were not available I doubt very much whether there would have been the division which has taken place. I therefore express my wonder that he who has received credit for having been the inventor of this plan should now, like so many inventors in the past, decline to share in the profits from that invention.
I pointed out then that the recognition of parties other than the official opposition in the manner I have already indicated was contrary to the basic principle of British parliamentary government, the contemplation of which has always been two parties; a party which governs, and a party in the opposition composed of the largest group. Again I wonder whether the chickens have not come home to roost somewhat earlier than expected. I expressed the fear that this measure might lead to a multiplicity and proliferation of parties in the days ahead. Certainly whatever the cause, the result is as I had anticipated.
If the committee is set up this party will be represented thereon and will make such decisions as in the wisdom of its membership are in keeping with the responsibilities that will rest on the committee. Certainly this committee, with all the potential problems that will be before it, will require all of the wisdom of a Solomon to carry out all the facets of the undertaking that will be theirs.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
maintopic: STATEMENT BY MR. SPEAKER RESPECTING SEATING ARRANGEMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we on this side are happy to support the motion which has been moved and which has been based on the suggestion you made to the house in such impressive terms. We are also grateful to you for the research you have done on this important subject. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) was good enough to comment on that research in impartial and objective terms. He has reminded the house, in terms which were not too flattering to some of his fellow members and which I think are regrettable, that some chickens are coming home to roost.
He has also reminded us of his prescience and his wisdom in the debate last July on the legislation to which he referred. But I should like to recall the circumstances of that particular debate to the right hon. gentleman, and remind him that in respect of this particular provision and all other provisions in that legislation he managed to find only five of his own party to support him in the house, and those five did not include a single member of his front bench or of his former colleagues in his government. I also recall that 28902-5-193
Seating Arrangements in Chamber although he had the opportunity he did not move a single amendment to any provision of that bill, including the provision to which he now takes such strong exception; and when I asked him during the debate if he intended to move that this legislation, to which he was then taking exception, be referred to a committee where it could be considered he disclaimed any such intention and did not take advantage of the suggestion I made. Therefore it is a little late for the right hon. gentleman to be so wise in respect of this particular measure.

maintopic: STATEMENT BY MR. SPEAKER RESPECTING SEATING ARRANGEMENTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, not only on behalf of the Social Credit party-

maintopic: STATEMENT BY MR. SPEAKER RESPECTING SEATING ARRANGEMENTS
speechtext: Which one?

maintopic: STATEMENT BY MR. SPEAKER RESPECTING SEATING ARRANGEMENTS
speechtext:
-of Canada but also on behalf of myself I wish to thank you for the thoughtful statement you have just made to us. I think it outlines the situation very well, and I agree with your suggestion that it is logical that this situation should go before a committee. The problem is not an easy one for you to decide.
I recall well the discussions we had before the first session of the former parliament began regarding the party order within the house, and I concur in the statement of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre that it was agreed at that time that on the basis of numbers the Social Credit party should take second precedence among the opposition parties. I believe that the proposition he has presented in his motion, provided it is in order, is reasonable.
However, the problem we have before us now is not really just the consideration of who or what a party is. It comes down to the fact that there are a number of people who as far as we know-their views have been expressed only in the press-have decided to break from the party which it is my privilege and responsibility to lead, and that in no way alters the status of the national Social Credit party. On this basis, Mr. Speaker, unless you have some direct word from the members concerned, it would seem to me that you would have to take the action you have taken. The situation comes down to this, that a number of members of our party have chosen to separate themselves from us, and thus they stand before us officially as a group of independents.
It is not for me to define what a party is or what should constitute a party, but there has been considerable discussion in this regard on other occasions. It has been brought out on a number of occasions, particularly with regard to the allotting of time for political broadcasting on the C.B.C., and it has generally been agreed that a party must be

Seating Arrangements in Chamber one that has contested an election and that has fielded candidates for at least half the number of seats in the nation and has been successful in winning some of those seats.
It is my opinion that you have recommended correctly, and we will concur in the motion that is before us so that this matter can go before a committee. You can be assured, Mr. Speaker, that we will give you our wholehearted support whatever the decision may be. In fairness to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, who has been speaking on behalf of the New Democratic party, on the basis of discussions we have had in the past I likewise agree that his statement is correct and that the party having the largest number of seats, provided it is a party, should be placed in the order of its numerical strength. On this basis I agree with the action you have taken and will support the motion that has been placed before the house.

maintopic: STATEMENT BY MR. SPEAKER RESPECTING SEATING ARRANGEMENTS
speechtext: Where is your leader?

maintopic: STATEMENT BY MR. SPEAKER RESPECTING SEATING ARRANGEMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette) will return to Ottawa around five o'clock this afternoon.
I listened closely to the remarks made earlier on this motion by the leader of the official opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker), and I wondered whether he realized that what is happening today to the former Social Credit leader might also happen to him before long. It was rather shabby of him to mention that the leader of the government had rightly termed the matter of the $4,000 which could have affected the decision. I must point out to him that when that question was put to the house last July, the hon. member for Villeneuve voted against it on second reading, just as he did himself; which goes to prove that opposites attract one another.
The reference made concerning the hon. member for Villeneuve reminded me of the saying by Pascal to the effect that everything is evil to the evil-minded.
Mr. Speaker, we think it is our duty if possible to support the motion introduced by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), but there is one thing which I noticed in your memorandum, upon which I would like to draw your attention:
Are we facing a new party and, if so, has it been officially recognized by the house? I think it is up to the house to decide that question.
As far as we are concerned, we believe that it is not up to a political or other party to decide whether a group of members who want to form a political party have the right to do so. That is a matter for the voters to decide, if they wish their elected members to form a political party.

The voters in our ridings have elected us under the Social Credit label and so we remained. That is a well-known and officially recognized fact. We are and remain in the Social Credit, that is seventeen members who have been elected under the label of the Social Credit rally. We are therefore a group recognized by the Canadian people, by the supporters of that political party. As the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre said, the party which is the most numerous enjoys certain privileges in the house. Therefore, I think that the Social Credit, that is the Social Credit rally should be recognized as a third opposition party in the house. As the New Democratic party numbers 17 members, we do not claim to take their place. I only want to mention one thing, Mr. Speaker, in closing my remarks, that is there are, none the less, in this house, 24 members who believe in Social Credit, and they are more numerous than those who follow socialist principles.
I hope that when the committee on privileges and elections makes its recommendations and a decision is taken, there will not be so many changes in the house.

speechtext: Has the Minister of Finance or the privy council office any precedents, exact or analogous, to the hiring of outside contractors for help in preparing the budget and, if so, what are they in terms of persons, dates and minutes passed and orders issued?

subtopic: * HIRING OF OUTSIDE CONTRACTORS FOR BUDGET PREPARATION

Knox, Kingston, Ontario, was appointed temporarily as assistant to the deputy minister of finance, to assist in the making of current estimates and forecasts of Canada's foreign exchange situation, and to be paid out of pocket living and travelling expenses.

DISCUSSIONS BETWEEN U.S. AND CANADA
speechtext: Are any matters currently under discussion or negotiation with the government of the United States of America or any agency or branch thereof, regarding the interest of both the U.S. and Canada or of interest only to Canada, and, if so, what specifically are these matters?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: DISCUSSIONS BETWEEN U.S. AND CANADA
speechtext: Discussions and negotiations on matters of common interest are being carried on continuously between the government of Canada and the government of the United States. It would be contrary to the public interest and to generally accepted practice to describe them while they are in progress or to specify all the subjects being discussed or negotiated. Both governments are, of course, conscious of the necessity for keeping the public well informed, and wherever discussions have matured to the point where a public announcement can be made this is done and, in particular, the house is appropriately informed.

CANADIAN WORKERS IN NEW ENGLAND STATES
speechtext:
1.	Does the government have statistics concerning Canadian workers employed in the states of Maine, New Hampshire, New York and Vermont each year from 1955 to 1963?
2.	Have agreements been entered into between Canadian and American authorities with respect to the payment of U.I.C. benefits to Canadian workers employed in the states of New York and Vermont and, if so, what is the nature of such agreements?

subtopic: CANADIAN WORKERS IN NEW ENGLAND STATES
speechtext:
1. Information regarding the number of Canadian workers employed in the states of Maine, New Hampshire, New York and Vermont for the years 1955 to 1963 is not available in so far as the Department of Labour and the unemployment insurance commission are concerned.
2. Yes. These agreements provide that a person who has acquired a right to benefit in Canada, who moves to either the state of New York or Vermont and who becomes unemployed while residing there, may make a claim against Canada by visiting the local unemployement compensation office, of the state, nearest to his residence and completing an application for benefit. That office sends the application to Canada, where eligibility is determined.
The claimant reports to the state office each week and makes a declaration as to his being unemployed the previous week. This
Questions
declaration is forwarded by the state office to Canada, which then makes payment direct to the claimant.
Conversely, a person who has acquired a right to benefit in either New York or Vermont, who moves to Canada and who becomes unemployed while residing there may make a claim, against the state concerned, by visiting the nearest local office of the unemployment insurance commission in Canada and completing an application for benefit. The unemployment insurance commission office forwards the application to the state concerned, where eligibility is determined.
The claimant reports to the unemployment insurance commission office each week and makes a declaration as to his being unemployed the previous week. This declaration is sent by the unemployment insurance commission office to the state concerned, which then makes payment direct to the claimant.
In summary, Canada acts as agent in taking claims for New York or Vermont for persons residing in Canada who have acquired benefit rights in either of these two states. On the other hand, these two states act as Canada's agent in taking claims for persons residing in those states and who have acquired benefit rights in Canada.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR PARLIA- MENTARY CONSIDERATION OF AGREEMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Prime Minister and ask him whether it is the intention of the government to lay before parliament for approval the agreement recently signed by the Canadian and United States governments regarding the conditions under which nuclear warheads would be made available to Canadian forces.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: NUCLEAR WARHEADS
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR PARLIA- MENTARY CONSIDERATION OF AGREEMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank my hon. friend for giving me notice of his question. The answer is in the negative. The customary and appropriate constitutional procedures have been followed in respect of this matter, which has already been discussed in the House of Commons.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. maintopic: INQUIRIES AS TO SALE TO RUSSIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would be very happy to answer this question. I received notice from the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam that he would ask the same question. Although the feasibility of using Churchill for shipments to the Soviet union was a matter of discussion between the Canadian wheat board and officials of the U.S.S.R., it was not found possible to use Churchill as a port of exit for the grain recently sold to that country. This important port has a

heavy program for this navigation season, and it is expected that Churchill will have a record high volume of wheat movement this year. I have before me the figures of recent movement, and for those who are familiar with the subject the estimated movement for this crop season will be 22,500,000 bushels, which I think everyone will recognize is a new record. The Soviet union required shipment prior to the opening of the 1964 Churchill navigation season, and the contracts were drawn up accordingly.
The government is very anxious to maximize the movement of wheat through Churchill. It is very conscious of the advantages of moving wheat in that direction, not only to the farmers but in order to reach as high a volume of exports as possible this season. The Canadian wheat board have advised that they are still prepared to enter into further commitments for shipment out of Churchill this fall. Account must be taken, however, of the buyers' wishes in this regard, and to date the fact is that no buyer has been prepared to charter vessels for Churchill that would involve movement beyond October 20. In this connection marine insurance is increased on October 15 and no insurance is available after October 20.

speechtext:
If we have, as I hope, concluded the questions on orders of the day I wonder, in view of the fact that no business was indicated for the house at the time we adjourned, if I could say a word about the business for today. I had hoped, and I made approaches to the representatives of hon. gentlemen opposite, that there would be consent to taking as the first item today the resolution, notice of which has been given to the Clerk, concerning the amendment to the Old Age Security Act. This would require unanimous consent, and I was not able to get an indication that there would be unanimous consent forthcoming.
However, sir, if I may I should like to point out that it is the desire of the government to have this legislation, if the house is willing to deal with it, dealt with rapidly so that the increase contemplated in the legislation may be made in the present month without having to be made retrospectively. I believe the cheques actually go out about the twentieth of the month. I believe all hon. members appreciate the difficulty of getting the parliamentary time to deal with these things. If there were any disposition on the part of hon. members to permit the hon. lady to advance the resolution to the stage where it could be debated, that is permit the house to go into committee and debate the resolution only, we would be prepared to do that.

We of course, would not ask the house to deal with the bill today. If we could dispose of the resolution, which is in very simple language, it would expedite what I believe everyone in the house is agreed, is a desirable objective.

speechtext: Agreed.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN AMOUNT OF PAYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very glad to see that the government is desirous of paying old age pensioners this additional $10 a month. It was the opposition that pointed out, over and over again, that the undertaking to do this was given during the election campaign, but when we dealt with this matter on July 18 last it was made very clear to us that the $10 increase would not be given unless the legislation covering the Canada pension plan was brought into effect.
Since then there has been a change of heart. The burning of conscience has brought about an alteration in the thinking of the government. I would point out this fact, Mr. Speaker, that we are most desirous of assuring the old age pensioners of that which they were promised and which we insist should be implemented.
I would further point out that the resolution introduced by the Minister of National Health and Welfare, as recorded at page 2340 of Hansard for July 18, among other things said:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to establish a comprehensive pension program to be known as the Canada pension plan-
Then a little later it said:
-for the payment of an additional pension of ten dollars a month to all persons to whom a pension may be paid under the Old Age Security Act.
And so on.
It will be recalled, sir, that in order to give the house an opportunity to recommend immediate payment to the government, and in compliance with the undertaking made by various hon. members now belonging to the government, I moved an amendment, seconded by the hon. member for Perth (Mr. Monteith), as recorded at page 2363 of Hansard for the same date:
That the said resolution-
-the resolution to which I have already made reference-
-be amended by adding after the words "ten dollars a month" in line 9:
"and this house asks that the government give consideration to making the payment of such additional pension to commence on this date."
The amendment was moved and the Deputy Speaker said he would have to take the question under advisement. The matter is still before the house and there has been no ruling

by the Deputy Speaker. Therefore there has been no opportunity for the house to give consideration to this amendment.
While we certainly welcome with open arms the conversion of the government to the needs of the old age pensioners, we ought to keep the proceedings of parliament regular. What about this amendment? It was not acceptable in July. The minister stated that under no circumstances could there be separation. That was before there was any question of any of the provinces refusing to participate in the plan.
Now we have a new situation, but the resolution of July is apparently forgotten about. Mr. Lesage has said he will not join in the proposition, and if newspaper reports are correct, according to one of the ministers of the government his action in that regard places him in a very unsatisfactory position, when a fund is built up, of being a follower of national socialism or nazism.
So far as Ontario is concerned, the ministers have met and they have discussed the matter. Surely then we ought to have a report on the proceedings to date. What is the present position? What has happened to the resolution that was rushed into with such a flash of arms and with such trumpet calls? The trumpet has a different sound now-an uncertain sound. Mr. Lesage has taken one blow on the trumpet and other provinces want an opportunity to do the same. What is the reason for this great change, this metamorphosis?

We also want information about the Canada pension plan. There are a great many things we want to know, but we will not get the information on orders of the day. The thing to do is let the government bring down its resolution and then, when we go into committee of the whole, we can question the minister and get a statement from the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN AMOUNT OF PAYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am privileged today on behalf of the government to introduce a measure calling for an increase in the old age security benefit from $65 to $75 a month, effective October 1, 1963. The last such increase in the fiat rate pension to our older citizens, from $55 to $65, was approved in this house 19 months ago.
You will have realized, Mr. Chairman, that the introduction of this resolution was made both necessary and urgent by recent developments respecting the Canada pension plan. It was originally the government's intention that the $10 increase in the old age security benefit be paid out of contributions to the Canada pension plan. When this house recessed two months ago, it was still our announced intention to present the necessary legislation at as early a date as possible.
Then, consequent upon the decision of the government of Quebec to forego the Canada pension plan in favour of a contributory plan of its own, it became evident to one and all that the part of the federal plan providing an increase in the flat rate pension had to be separated from the rest of the scheme. Contributions raised in provinces participating in the federal plan obviously cannot be used to provide benefits in a province from which no such contributions are forthcoming. That is the situation today and it is the aim of the subject amendment to provide the additional $10 benefit to all provinces, irrespective of the Canada pension plan.
I might mention here that section 94A of the British North America Act was designed to provide for concurrent jurisdiction in the field of old age pensions and that the future development of pension arrangements over and beyond the universal flat rate pension will depend upon mutually satisfactory arrangements being worked out. In the case of the province of Quebec there is a preference for a provincial contributory plan. The possibility of developing an earnings-related pension plan for the rest of Canada will

depend upon the attitude of the other provinces and, in particular, Ontario which already has legislation on the statute books dealing with a pension plan. The federal goverment has made clear the kind of Canadawide plan it believes would provide adequate old age income security for Canadians. The onus now rests with the other provinces as to whether we proceed with this plan.
The present pensionable age under the Old Age Security Act is 70 years. As you may be aware, Mr. Chairman, it has been the government's hope, as expressed in earlier statements made in this house respecting the Canada pension plan, to make reduced benefits available to old age pensioners who desire them on a graduated scale, between ages 65 and 70. As already announced, under the Canada pension plan these reduced benefits would apply both to the flat rate pension and to benefits under the earnings-related plan.
The question of age adjusted benefits, both with respect to graduated and flat rate pensions, is a matter which will be the subject of discussions with the provinces and, in particular, with the provinces of Quebec and Ontario with respect to their plans for pension arrangements. The government will give this aspect further consideration following these discussions and if, as we hope, the outcome of these negotiations is successful, the matter will be considered at the time the Canada pension legislation is placed before this house.
In the meantime the present pension increase will result in a substantial rise in expenditure under the Old Age Security Act on behalf of some 960,000 pensioners. At the present figure of $65 a month, the over-all expenditure for the fiscal year 1963-64 would be $750 million; for the year 1964-65, with a normal increase in the number of pensioners, the figure would be $766 million.
At the proposed rate of $75 per month, effective October 1, 1963, the expenditure for the fiscal year 1963-64 would be $807 million; for 1964-65, it would be $882 million. Now, therefore, the difference for the year 1964-65 between expenditures at the present rate and at the proposed rate of $75 per month would be $116 million. This raises a question as to the source of the additional revenue for this increased expenditure. You will be hearing more about this a little later from my colleague, from the Department of Finance.
This present measure is, Mr. Chairman, a solid step in the right direction, but the government sincerely hopes that the Canada pension plan will be introduced before too long to provide adequately for the retirement of our older people. I am confident that this present amendment will be followed by further measures which will in fact provide that

added cushion of security and dignity so richly deserved by our senior citizens.

This is certainly a different type of approach, a very humble approach today, compared with her speech on July 18. At that time she went into much detail ridiculing the
Old Age Security
opposition for their efforts in social security, which over the years have certainly been much more beneficial to the senior citizens than those of the present government.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I want to review one or two things the previous government did in its short term of office, a period of five and a half to six years. In that time the old age security and related benefits were increased by $19 a month. This was done in two stages. The government of that day had no sooner taken office than it proposed an increase of $9 a month, which was one of the most pleasant duties I had to perform as minister of national health and welfare. This proposal was acceded to by the house, unanimously I believe. The previous government did that following the almost abortive attempt in the previous spring to do something for the elderly citizens. At that time the then minister of finance proposed an increase of $6 a month. We knew what that meant. We knew how inadequate it was. We appreciated the fact that the elderly citizens should have had more than this. As a consequence, when we came into office we immediately proposed this $9 increase. This was in November 1957 and it became effective that month. Then in the spring of 1962, effective I believe on February 1, there was a further increase in old age security of $10 a month which the previous government felt was necessary at the time.
We are also very much in favour of this increase, as exemplified by the amendment of the Leader of the Opposition on July 18. I think that this proves that our party, the previous government, has had the welfare of the elder citizens uppermost in mind and has certainly done everything possible to relieve the hardship which these people suffer.
During my term of office, Mr. Chairman, I had many meetings with the elder citizen groups. I know the present minister has undoubtedly had similar meetings also. I came to believe, however, that the country as a whole does not appreciate the real plight of many of these people in the circumstances under which they live. I feel that the present suggestion is not only necessary but is delayed. This could have been achieved and could have been effective as of last August 1 at the latest, if the present government had only listened to the suggestion put forward by the Leader of the Opposition at that time.
Instead of that the present minister was imbued with political venom. In fact, she reminded me of the Minister of Finance in his budget speech debate; they were two of a kind. The Minister of Finance had to make some retreats following that, and it is obvious what has happened in this case. The present Minister of National Health and Welfare has had to make a retreat. Perhaps she has seen

Old Age Security
the light; I hope it is for that reason. I was not in the house at the moment but I understand she indicated that the change in this respect was because of the attitude of the province of Quebec. During recent efforts in the province of Ontario she did not indicate that this might be the reason for her change, quite so much as she was trying to indicate, I think, that the present government of Ontario might be wholly responsible for this change in attitude. I have seen flip-flaps and that sort of thing in the past, Mr. Chairman, but I do not know when I have seen two more striking examples than the Minister of Finance in his budget speech and the present Minister of National Health and Welfare when she introduced the original resolution on July 18.

subtopic: MOTION RESPECTING TRANSFER OF JURISDICTION
speechtext:
Well, they have said on previous occasions that neither the minister nor the department has any responsibility for wheat sales. We do not believe that to be the case, but since it was the hon. members opposite who made that statement they cannot very well contradict what they have told the public on previous occasions-or can they? We would, I am sure, be pleased to have the minister tell this house and the Canadian public in general exactly how these wheat sales are made. There can be no doubt that the Canadian wheat board is under the sole control of the government and that it is the only marketing agency for wheat produced in western Canada. As westerners, we have been amazed at times at the interpretation which the people of eastern Canada have placed on the transactions of the Canadian wheat board. They do not seem to realize that it is the

sole marketing agency lor our grain. I was surprised to hear comments which indicated that even some members of this house thought that every time an initial payment was paid to western producers it came out of the Canadian treasury. Such an impression is entirely wrong. Under the marketing system through which western Canadian grain is sold, that payment represents the farmers' own money.
In trying to get some information with regard to the actions of the Canadian wheat board I have looked up a number of editorials which have appeared in eastern as well as western papers. I should like to read parts of these editorials-I do not intend to read them all-in order to illustrate my contention. I shall refer first of all to an editorial which appeared in the Calgary Herald on April 24, 1963, right after the general election. This editorial is headed: "New Wheat Board Management" and it says:
The federal department of agriculture over which Hon. Harry Hays of Calgary is to preside as minister will differ in two major respects from its Conservative counterpart.
The article goes on to discuss the changes briefly-I shall not read it all-and then it says:
The wisdom of these two Liberal changes will be determined by the future course of events. At the outset they appear to be good ones.
When the retired minister of agriculture, Alvin Hamilton, had the wheat board operations transferred to his jurisdiction in 1960, complaints were rife that the trade department had not been devoting sufficient effort to wheat sales abroad. It was alleged that time and effort which should have been going into wheat disposal were being devoted to consultations and arguments between the wheat board and the trade department on policy and procedure.
Certainly, after Mr. Hamilton took the wheat board under his wing there was a speedy revitalization of wheat sales. Credit agreements were negotiated abroad and, along with a fortuitously light Canadian crop in 1961 and a famine in China, sales zoomed and surpluses declined.
Actually, when we were selected the majority of Conservative members from the west had one major problem. As grain politicians we were careful; we did not make too many promises to the western people. But one promise I made was this: I undertook to do all I could to help the Canadian government solve the problem of surplus grain. At the time I made the promise I was not too much concerned about which party would form the government. As I hope to show in a few moments, I criticized our own party, which formed the government at that time, for its attitude with regard to the Canadian wheat board. As I have indicated, along with others I made the promise that we would try to solve this surplus grain problem. Today, in the light of political statements which have been made
Canadian Wheat Board by ministers and others, people are still confused as to who does actually make these sales. This confusion has existed for some time. I am not sure whether the former minister said he made the sales or not. I do know that the opposition definitely said he did not. But somebody did make these sales, and all I have to say today to whoever was responsible is that this sale of wheat to Russia has done Canada a lot of good.
The editorial from which I have been reading goes on to say:
But if previous sales efforts had been less than successful, the blame largely could be laid at the door of the trade department which was concerned with trying to push industrial and commercial sales to the neglect of agricultural products.
Under the new leadership of Hon. Mitchell Sharp however, the Department of Trade and Commerce is not likely to make the same mistake.
I question that statement, and I do so in the light of the previous record of the Canadian wheat board at a time when Canada was losing sales on the world market. The present Minister of Trade and Commerce was then the deputy minister responsible for the department, and unless he has changed his ways with respect to western agriculture and sales of western grain we shall revert to placing this board under the direction of the Department of Trade and Commerce which, I say, would be a retrograde step.
In order to show hon. members what the thinking of eastern people is with regard to western farmers I should like to refer to an editorial which appeared in the Toronto Globe and Mail dated August 13, 1963. I presume this paper could be considered as being a supporter of the Conservative party, while the other paper to which I have referred, the Calgary Herald, could be considered a supporter of the Liberal party. I do not know for certain but I imagine from the comments made that this would be correct. The article in the Globe and Mail was written by Scott Young, who apparently had been out west. He was writing about western Conservatives and about the wheat situation out there. He referred to a feeling that the Dief-enbaker government had demonstrated an understanding of the west's problems, and said:
As long as he leads the Conservatives no other party is going to make five cents worth of progress out here.
I think that is correct. Referring to the promise made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) regarding $2 a bushel for wheat, the article says:
The nonsensical quality of the promise was strongly demonstrated by the trade minister's rather petulant suggestion that westerners should grow less wheat.

Canadian Wheat Board
I do not think the minister denies that he went out west and told the farmers union, in Edmonton, I think it was: Do not grow more wheat, because we cannot sell what you are already producing. This Russian sale makes that statement sound somewhat ridiculous. I have contended all along as a representative from western Canada that whoever is responsible for selling wheat, whether it be the grain board or the Department of Agriculture or the Department of Trade and Commerce, is doing so as an agency of the government itself. Selling wheat is a government responsibility, and if it cannot sell it the western people must be told so.
Now I shall read from what is, I presume, a Liberal paper. This seems to reflect the attitude of a number of eastern people. Commenting in the Kingston Whig-Standard on Mr. Young's article, the writer says:
But, quite apart from politics, this business of wheat in the west is obviously something concerning which Mr. Young has let the farmers out there talk him into a daze. The western wheat farmer has no interest in what kind of a market he has for his wheat; all he cares about is selling it at as high a price as possible. It is, he thinks, his God given right and destiny to grow and sell wheat-this is the heart of the western mythology. ...They don't want to work any harder than that and they betray no hesitation in saying so.
That is absolutely ridiculous. If this is the opinion that the government or the Liberal party has of western wheat producers, it will be a long, long time before they will have sufficient members from the prairies to appoint a minister of agriculture from that region. They were quite fortunate last time.

subtopic: MOTION RESPECTING TRANSFER OF JURISDICTION
speechtext: I don't know that they were.

subtopic: MOTION RESPECTING TRANSFER OF JURISDICTION
speechtext:
I also want to refer to another eastern paper which I think has an actual grasp of what the situation is in the west. This is the story that I am quite sure western Canada wants to put across to eastern Canada, because it is true, and if anybody wants to take the time to delve into the subject he will find it is so. I wish to refer to the Sudbury Daily Standard of June 20, 1963. The article is headed, "Farmers Fear New Policies Will Damage Export Markets", and it reads in part as follows:
Revelation that the Pearson government in Ottawa hired "outside" experts to assist in the preparation of the budget should not be surprising. Informed Canadians know that there is sometimes little relation between Liberal election propaganda and performance.
The most recent election campaign was no exception. This was the party of "experts" in the matter of economics; this was the party with the men of ideas "to get the economy rolling". But once in office the Liberals hired experts "outside" of government and the civil service.
Nor is this delusion on Liberal know-how confined to matters of finance. One section of the farm press that came out strongly in support of the 
Liberal party and urged a change in government is now having second thoughts, and nearly all published letters written by farmers disagree with the Liberal policies. It is now a matter of record that the farm vote in Canada was almost solidly in support of the Diefenbaker government.
It may be remembered that Liberal government dairy policies were made known only 36 hours before the May 1 deadline and decisions on policy changes made only some 50 hours after agriculture minister Harry Hays and agriculture minister-to-be Rene Tremblay took their oaths of office.
The farm press has been taking a long, hard look at these policies which indicate greater dairy surpluses, lower exports, higher prices to consumers and reduced income for dairy farmers. It is feared there will be serious export loss in British and European markets. The Liberals, who favour more trade with the United States, cannot look for markets for farm products in that country. It is already plagued with stockpiled surpluses.
It will also be remembered that in its first days of office the Liberal government returned the Canadian wheat board to the Department of Trade and Commerce.
This is significant? It could be. The Diefenbaker government put the board under the Department of Agriculture and export wheat sales soared. By midMay, under the Liberals, export wheat sales were already down by 30 million bushels from the same time last year. There seems to be little likelihood that the Liberal government will be able to match the Diefenbaker government's record in wheat exports.
That would have been correct had it not been for the one sale to Russia. I will prove later with figures that under the Liberal administration, whether they were the ones who sold wheat or whether the wheat board under their direction sold wheat, Canada was gradually losing all her foreign markets for wheat. The article goes on to say:
Canadian wheat farmers also have long memories They can recall a previous Liberal administration that lost Canadian wheat sales by trying to collect another five cents a bushel from prospective European customers. It was a Liberal administration that tried to unload Canadian wheat at $1.50 a bushel when the world market price was $3. a bushel.
I think that is sufficient information from the press to convey to the house that the issue is a very confusing one, and the government by its action of putting the wheat board back under the Department of Trade and Commerce has confused the issue more. When the wheat board was under the Department of Trade and Commerce at the time that the present minister was deputy minister the policies were also confused.
I have mentioned before that I was very critical of our party in this regard. I refer to page 7693 of Hansard tor August 6, 1960, at which time I said:
As the government has complete control of the marketing of wheat on the prairies, then it is the responsibility of the government to see that markets are obtained or tell the producers they are unable to do the job.

I also said at that time:
I have reason to believe that the present wheat board policy in determining its daily selling price for Canadian wheat offerings to domestic and foreign buyers is too rigid, and that as a result of this inflexibility we have lost foreign sales which should have been available to our western producers. I am aware that those who do not agree with my remarks will charge that I am trying to interfere with the orderly system of marketing western grain. I hasten to say that if such a system solves or will solve the problem of the western grain surplus, then I will support it wholeheartedly.
In talking about the western grain surplus I may say that there are other problems created because there is a surplus. There is the problem of cash advances on farm stored grain. There is the problem of quotas. There is the problem of the allocation of box cars. I am quite sure that the present Minister of Trade and Commerce has some knowledge of what these problems are, particularly with regard to cash advances on farm stored grain, because I understand that under the Liberal administration he was one of those who said it could not be done. It was one of the first things that was done under the Conservative administration when they took office in 1957. I continue:
On the other hand, if the present orderly system of marketing works to the disadvantage of the western grain producers whom I represent, then I suggest that some of the conditions in this system should be changed.
I am not advocating that the orderly system of marketing should be discarded. I believe I am offering evidence that proves that the way it is functioning at the present time can lead to only one result, the loss of further grain markets for our producers. It is essential that we avoid this downward pattern.
To show what the downward trend was we did a lot of research at that time. On that occasion I said, as found on page 7692 of Hansard for August 6, 1960:
I would draw your attention, Mr. Chairman, to the grain trade year book, which indicates that in some foreign markets Canada's grain sales were reduced by a considerable amount during the grain year 1958-59 from those of the previous grain year.
I went on to say:
I have also before me a table which shows that during the past year Russia exported 40 million bushels of wheat to western European countries, and many of these countries were former customers of Canada. It is to be noted that Canadian wheat sales to the Netherlands dropped from 21 million bushels in 1957-58 to 7 million bushels in 1958-59. That is an actual decline of 14 million bushels in one year in sales to one of our most valuable customers.
I should say that at that time under a Conservative administration the wheat board was also under the Department of Trade and Commerce and it was later that the decision was made to transfer it to the Department of Agriculture. I went on to say:
28902-5-195
Canadian Wheat Board
During that same period, 1958-59, Russia sold to the Netherlands almost 10 million bushels of wheat. ...It is also to be noted that Sweden purchased over 2 million bushels of wheat from Russia during 1958-59-
And so it goes on and on. If you wish to pursue the matter further you will see that in practically every country with which we had been dealing we were losing out as far as the export of Canadian grain was concerned, and Russia was gaining on us. What we seemed to lose the Russians apparently were taking over. This not only applied to all European countries but also to the United Kingdom. Our research also proved that we were losing out in the case of the United Kingdom. It also proved that world demand had increased from 660 million bushels, prior to the war, to 1,220 million bushels. In fact, the demand for wheat was growing constantly but Canadian exports to world markets were declining. Whose fault was that? Was that the fault of the government or was it the fault of the Canadian wheat board? I am not too sure that we have the answer. I will say this, that after similar speeches were made in this house when action was taken to transfer the Canadian wheat board from the Department of Trade and Commerce to the Department of Agriculture, something happened. Markets for Canadian grain became available. I am quite sure Canadian producers do not care who was responsible or who gets credit for that. The grain was sold.
As I mentioned before, we solved the problem of surplus grain and the problems related to surplus grain such as storage, quotas, box car allocations, cash advances and everything else. It is for this reason I say a retrograde step was taken in transferring the wheat board back to-

Since the motion was introduced in English, I think it would be appropriate for me to give the first half of my speech in English. As we understand it, the present question is not a question of philosophy, of political, economic or administrative theory, it is a question of efficiency. The question is: Can the Department of Trade and Commerce sell wheat more effectively than the Department of Agriculture? The opposition, of course, takes the negative view.
In my opinion, the question is one of common sense, so I will proceed in a common sense manner. I should like to preface my remarks with three notes. The first is this: The question is not one related to the growing

Canadian Wheat Board of wheat but to the sale of it. We understand that the growing of wheat is the business of the farmers, and the Department of Agriculture can advise them on this matter. However, the question is about the sale of wheat, the trade in wheat, and of course we believe this matter should come under the Department of Trade and Commerce.

On that subject the minister said this in a speech on September 23:
I am sure that you would wish the government to recognize the wheat board and its chief officer in this way. The Canadian wheat board is given responsibility by parliament for marketing western wheat, oats and barley and it is important that this responsibility should not be usurped by any minister of the crown.
This is quite clear.
The government does have a responsibility in the marketing of western grain and that is to support the wheat board and to create the conditions under which the board can sell wheat, oats and barley to best advantage.
Referring to the sale to communist China, the minister went on to say that the government's role was to improve the terms of access for Chinese goods, and to underwrite the extension of credit, both of which were essential to the successful outcome. This is the function of the government, and this is the function of the Department of Trade and Commerce, to help the wheat board in selling wheat. We Liberals do recognize the importance of the wheat board. We also recognize the importance of God in connection with these sales. There is no doubt about it-an act of God can be negative or positive-without an act of God these sales might not have taken place, no matter how good our sales department is. This attitude, I believe, is quite clear. I think you will find it very difficult to find any other than the one I am expressing now.

speechtext: I should like now to state my three main arguments in favour of the present arrangement. The first one is related to history, and it goes like this. The wheat board does as well, if not better, under trade and commerce now as it did under agriculture at the time that department was headed by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle.
My second point is that wheat cannot be treated as something entirely apart from general trade. You cannot isolate the trade in wheat from the general preoccupation of the government in respect of trade. Negotiations in relation to world trade are not divided into compartments. For example, in the GATT negotiations the preoccupation for agricultural products cannot be isolated. The over-all picture must be kept in mind by Canadian representatives.

Canadian Wheat Board
As you know, Mr. Speaker, Canada experiences great difficulties in the field of trade and we must at all cost put all advantages on our side. The authorities representing us in such large international negotiations must be able to make arrangements on the widest possible basis. Mr. Speaker, I also wish to call to the attention of the house the fact that the Department of Trade and Commerce has an excellent team of trade commissioners who are acting as scouts in every country of the world. subtopic: MOTION RESPECTING TRANSFER OF JURISDICTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would first like to congratulate the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. McIntosh) for moving his motion today so that it would give hon. members an opportunity to discuss some of the pros and cons respecting sales of Canadian wheat during the last few years.

Canadian Wheat Board
We know there has been an attempt, successful to some extent, to sell the idea to Canadian wheat farmers that they were immeasurably better off in terms of activity and efforts to sell their wheat when the Canadian wheat board was under the administration of the Department of Agriculture.
I do not believe any hon. member would deny that there was one single success of a size so large that it overshadowed many other sales during the period when the board came under the Department of Agriculture. But the next question which must be asked is whether those who wish the board transferred back to that department also want to give the department the responsibility for the great droughts in China and Canada in recent years? I do not think that is a valid argument, and I do not believe even those members of the Conservative party who support this motion would like to assume that responsibility.
The hon. member for Drummond-Artha-baska (Mr. Pepin) has mentioned that there are many other things which must be considered in addition to agricultural policy. For example all hon. members will agree that the last three very large wheat sales were directly tied to some credit arrangements and might not have been completed had it not been for the existence of these arrangements. I suggest that these credit arrangements can be handled just as successfully by the Department of Trade and Commerce and its minister as by the Minister of Agriculture. I am also sure it will be agreed that such a kind of agreement must be reached by the entire cabinet, and that there is no significant difference whether the Minister of Agriculture or the Minister of Trade and Commerce makes recommendations to the cabinet.
There are other trading arrangements involved in the sale of wheat. These were referred to by the hon. member who spoke just before me, and I have a whole stack of editorials and statements which I have gathered throughout the years, and which indicate without doubt that the leading grain spokesmen-if one wants to call them that-have over the years tried to convince the government that there is a direct relationship between trading policies respecting other commodities and the promotion of sales with regard to wheat.
For example I have before me a letter which appeared on the editorial page of the Winnipeg Free Press and which was sent to the former prime minister, Mr. Diefenbaker, by Mr. W. J. Parker, president of Manitoba pool elevators, on behalf of the Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba wheat pools and United Grain Growers Limited. I shall only read a few paragraphs from this letter to prove that what I have said is correct:

In concurrence with and on behalf of the United Grain Growers Limited, Alberta wheat pool, Saskatchewan wheat pool and Manitoba pool elevators, I desire to acquaint you with a matter which is causing grave concern among the combined membership of these producer organizations.
Doubtless you are aware that Japan has of recent years become our second largest market for wheat, and from time to time an important market for Canadian barley and oilseeds. It is the considered opinion of those in a position to judge that Japan will in the not too distant future become the largest market for Canadian wheat, provided Canada pursues a trade policy designed to encourage the purchase by Japan of cereals from us.
The letter concludes by saying:
I assure you, Mr. Prime Minister, that the farmers our organizations represent would appreciate assurance from you that the government is not attempting to reduce Japanese participation in the Canadian market in 1960 below the level obtaining in 1959 for any commodity, and that it remains the policy of your government year by year to increase each and every quota on Japanese imports, with a view to their eventual removal.
He mentioned earlier the problem of allowing customers for wheat to sell sufficient of their own products in Canada in order to earn Canadian dollars to pay for our wheat. This has been going on for so long that it is almost repetitious to mention it at this time. One reason advanced is that if we have the Department of Trade and Commerce directly involved in the selling of Canadian wheat we would also receive a more sympathetic response from them in advocating import quota increases, and so on, which would allow our customers to sell their goods in Canada to earn the dollars that are necessary. There are other matters, which were raised by the hon. member who spoke previously such as GATT and various other negotiations that are necessary. Surely, Mr. Speaker, no hon. member of this house will argue that all these integrated matters are primarily the responsibility of the Department of Trade and Commerce.
There is one other point. I refer to the matter of financing. I dealt with this subject briefly a few minutes ago. I have some quotations of what has been said by the previous minister of agriculture, now the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton), who stated that it was becoming increasingly difficult to get approval from his colleagues in the Conservative government for the credit necessary to finance some of these large scale sales. For example, in The Western Producer of November 15, 1962 there is this quotation:
Mr. Hamilton's speech reflected growing pressure against credit sales from eastern Canadians and those who do not understand the problems of the farmers.

The mover of the motion says, amongst other things, that it is a retrograde step to place the Canadian wheat board-which has, in addition to its original role, the administration of cash advances, acreage payments, the issuing of permit books, and the quota allocation-under the Minister of Trade and Commerce. Taking each one of these items separately, I think we should consider whether there was any distinct advantage in transferring this board to the Department of Agriculture. I might say, Mr. Speaker, that some ministers of agriculture even before the hon. member for Qu'Appelle stated that the Canadian wheat board was not under the direct direction, if you want to call it that, of any department; that they in fact pursued the policy of selling wheat almost independently of the government.
Then there is the matter of the administration of cash advances. In 1957, prior to placing the wheat board under the control of the Minister of Agriculture, I know of no difficulty that the board had in administering cash advances.

There may be some kind of argument as to whether or not the present government and its cabinet is going to authorize acreage payments at all. But whether they are administered by the Department of Trade and Commerce or the Department of Agriculture presents no significant difference that I can see.
With regard to the issuing of permit books, this was done by the Canadian wheat board for about 18 years prior to its being taken over by the Department of Agriculture.
