Quota allocation is something that comes about after taking several factors into consideration. One is the matter of having sold a certain grade of wheat and the requirements of the Canadian wheat board to get it into export position. For example-and this has happened on a number of occasions -they have sold a large quantity of No. 5 or No. 4 wheat and if there was a shipping point that had frost, or there was some other reason, and there was a large quantity of this kind of wheat and a sale was made, there was an effort on the part of the Canadian wheat board to move as much of that wheat as quickly as possible into export positions so that it could be delivered. Perhaps this comes under the Department of Transport to some extent, and I think the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) has just as free access to the Department of Transport as has the Minister of Agriculture. I can therefore see no significant improvement in this regard.
By and large, Mr. Speaker, I have to agree with the mover of the motion, the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. McIntosh) and the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska (Mr. Pepin) when they suggest that these administrative details are not of major concern. The major concern is to generate and enhance our over-all trading position in the international market so that we have more customers. We have to make some arrangements to take in some of the products of these other countries, and this is not easy. I know that even today there is some discontent in the textile industry. They are a little apprehensive that some of the sales made to China and Russia may have included an agreement, whether signed or not, which will mean there will be a flood of textiles into Canada to pay for some of this wheat. This is a matter of justifiable concern, but I am not convinced that the Minister of Agriculture could handle this problem any better than the Minister of Trade and Commerce. As a matter of fact I think all these integrated things could be better handled by a department that is totally concerned with trade and commerce.
The last thing I wish to say, Mr. Speaker, is that perhaps the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) also has something to contribute to the over-all sale of Canadian wheat in the international market. We know, for example,

Canadian Wheat Board that a number of suggestions have been put forward to the effect that we should accept some so-called soft currencies for Canadian wheat. We have heard that the United States, in competing in the international market, have in fact accepted local currencies and have left those currencies in the countries to be used in the form of foreign aid. If we are going to try to compete with the United States on this basis, I suggest the Department of Finance will also have a very large say in the matter.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I can see no great advantage in adopting this motion and I can in fact see some disadvantages, one of which would be perhaps losing a little of the position we might have within the cabinet in having both the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Trade and Commerce responsible for advancing the welfare of agriculture through increased wheat sales.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak to this motion I see my time is limited. I should like to say a few things in support of the motion. Basically the crux of the problem is whether or not western Canada and the wheat board, the jurisdiction of which lies solely in western Canada, is represented by a western or an eastern minister. History will bear me out that over the years the minister of agriculture has always been a western member, although that may not be the case in the future. Therefore, I think the first point is that he should have a closer contact with the area within which the jurisdiction of the wheat board lies-western Canada, and western Canada alone.
We have heard the record of the pros and cons of the two boards as they operated under the two departments in years gone by. The hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska (Mr. Pepin) knew very little about what he was saying, because he compared sales of wheat and said that under a former government the wheat board sold as much wheat as they did in the last few years under the very able direction of the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton). Now, what is the case? In previous years the wheat board sold about 2 per cent of Canada's wheat under a former minister of agriculture and the Department of Agriculture. Under the direction of the hon. member for Qu'Appelle we sold by direct agreement up to 35 per cent of Canada's wheat. There is the difference between the two types of administration so far as the wheat board is concerned.
We have heard some talk about the various ministers. We westerners, and we western farmers in particular, know the record of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) with regard to the wheat board. What

did he say about cash advances? He said they were not necessary and could not be administered, that they would ruin the wheat board. What did the Right Hon. C. D. Howe say about wheat sales when he was minister of trade and commerce? He said if they want to buy wheat let them come and get it. That was the attitude of the then government and the then deputy minister of trade and commerce.
What did the hon. member for Qu'Appelle do for the wheat board? He convinced the cabinet that Canadian wheat should be sold on credit. That is a principle that has been established and is continued today by the present government: they are selling wheat on credit. This was never done before. Western farm delegations came to Ottawa during past years and asked the government to sell their wheat, to give credit. We amended the Export Credits Insurance Act to make possible the first sale of wheat to China. This new principle has been accepted and the Export Credits Insurance Act was the vehicle, you might say, by which the Russian sale was made possible.
It is very important to western Canada that the wheat board have control to a great extent of the economy of the farmers generally. And what do the farmers want? I have here an editorial which I should like to read. It says:
According to the national farmers' union, the government is wrong on two points of agricultural policy.
They are referring to the present government.
It should not appoint a second minister of agriculture to deal with the farm problems of eastern Canada.
Apparently the government has realized that and done away with the idea.
The wheat board, which sells all wheat, should not have been transferred from the Department of Agriculture to the Department of Trade and Commerce.
That is what the national farmers' union said about the action taken by the present government.
We have heard a lot of talk about the Russian and Chinese wheat agreements. Two basic principles were accepted and I hope will continue to be accepted, no matter which party forms the government. These principles were sales on credit and the acceptance of sterling. They are two important points which never before had been accepted by any minister of trade and commerce, and would not likely have been accepted today were it not for a hard-working and aggressive minister of agriculture who had the foresight to ask the cabinet to transfer the wheat board to his jurisdiction.

I must congratulate the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. McIntosh) for bringing forward this motion. He, along with other western members, convinced the government that wheat should be sold on credit if necessary; that if wheat were sold it would lift the burden off the backs of the western farmers generally. I am sure hon. members from western Canada will bear out that statement; it has lifted a tremendous burden from the backs of farmers generally in western Canada.
We have heard a lot of talk about the recept China wheat sale. The hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska referred to the part God had played. I am sure they are thankful for the part that somebody played because it came as a complete bombshell and surprise to them. I say that because the Minister of Trade and Commerce said, according to page 2562 of Hansard, during the question period for that day:
I say to the hon. member who has just interrupted, I do not think it helped greatly when the former minister suggested the farmers should grow all the wheat they could, and that he would sell it for them.
That is what he suggested to the farmers during the election. He did not suggest $2 a bushel for wheat as they suggested-a promise they knew could not be kept when they suggested it. The former minister said grow the wheat. He said we have now achieved credit sales and are accepting sterling. He was confident that through the continuation of his efforts and the efforts of the wheat board sales could be made and markets found. This house owes-certainly the western farmers owe-a great deal of appreciation for his hard work on their behalf. It is not like the present Minister of Trade and Commerce who travels out to western Canada even after a large wheat sale and tells the farmer not to grow any more wheat, to reduce their acreage because he cannot sell it. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays), like little Sir Echo, travels along with him and says: "Don't grow any more wheat; we can't sell it". What kind of attitude is this? The province of Saskatchewan is now considered the bread basket of the world. It is the only part of the world in which surplus wheat sales have been made possible through aggressive technological changes which the farmers have been ready to adopt in order to grow wheat and, in order to meet competition and the cost price squeeze they find themselves in today. Certainly-

The minister said on July 18:
Unfortunately, however, in recent years some of the increases in payments made under this legislation have been based not upon increase in productivity, not upon progress of the economy, but only upon pure political expediency. This can no longer be countenanced.
I have never seen such an example of political expediency as this particular move. Further, I would say that the whole matter has been ill prepared. We did not even have a copy of the resolution at the time this subject came up for discussion. Rightly or wrongly, it appeared to me that there was only one copy available and it seems that the rules, not to mention house etiquette, should provide for more.
I suggest we look at the resolution itself. It includes provision for raising the rate of old

age security tax from 3 per cent, with a maximum of $90, to 4 per cent with a maximum of $120 on the taxable income of individuals. I am sorry I was not in the house this afternoon when the minister spoke. I think we have been asked once again to buy a pig in a poke to pull this government out of a hole. I should like to know when these related acts are likely to be amended. I suggest this government should get its feet on the ground and find out where it is going. Those planners over there certainly lack any sense of planning in this case, though they are noted as being planners. In that speech on July 18, the minister made what appeared to me and, I think, to the public as a whole, to be some terribly biased political and partisan statements.

dealt with in the fall session of 1957 had to do with the increase in old age security benefits. We reduced the residence requirement from 20 years to ten years. Allowable earnings were increased. Early in 1958, in this field of social welfare, we removed the threshold of 45 per cent of provincial population under which the government could give unemployment assistance. We increased the rate from 40 per cent to 50 per cent by which we participated at that time. In those days there were only four or five provinces in the scheme. Subsequent to our amendment, all the provinces in Canada came into the arrangement. Early in 1958 we doubled hospital construction grants, increased nurses' accommodation grants, chronic hospital bed grants and added internes' accommodation and major alterations and renovations. Early in 1958 we amended the clause whereby a majority of the provinces representing a majority of the population had to have legislation on their books before there could be any hospital insurance in force in Canada. We brought in an amendment and by July 1, 1958, five provinces in Canada had hospital insurance and the citizens of Canada in those provinces were receiving the benefits of it. Subsequently all 10 provinces and the two territories joined in the scheme.
In 1960 we made it possible for the people of Canada to enjoy benefits while out of the country by allowing absences from Canada which had not been hitherto enjoyed. In the fall of 1961 we brought in the fitness and amateur sport program. In the spring of 1962 we amended the national health and welfare act to set up a national council on welfare. We introduced national welfare grants starting at $500,000 with increases of $500,000 a year to a maximum of $2,500,000. In February of 1962 we increased old age security payments by another $10 and also all related acts and, of course, there was a consequent increase in allowable earnings.
To me, sir, this represents a tremendous expansion in social security services in Canada. I should like to refer to some figures. In 1956-57, the last year of the Liberal government prior to the present one, health and welfare grants totalled $881 million. In 196263 they were $1.9 billion or an increase of 115 per cent. Health and welfare payments to provinces increased from $75 million in 1956-57 to $527 million in 1962-63, or an increase of 603 per cent. Health and welfare payments to individuals increased in the same period from $815 million to $1.4 billion,

or an increase of 72 per cent. If you will look at the books of estimates for the years 1956-57 and 1963-64 you will see that the total increase in health and welfare estimates is from $881 million to $1,959 billion, or 122 per cent.
Over a period of time the minister has tried to indicate that the efforts of the former government left something to be desired. I beg to point out that no government in the history of Canada has ever increased its social security payments to the people of Canada, or its social security measures, by as great an amount over a similar period.
I had the honour of bringing in the increase in old age security in the autumn of 1957 and I should like to point out the actual timetable of the discussions in that session. We brought it in in the proper legislative manner. Four resolutions were put on the order paper, one having to do with old age security, another with old age assistance, another with blindness allowances and the last one with disabled persons allowances. On Thursday, October 24, we discussed the first resolution on old age security. We further discussed it on Friday, October 25 and again on Thursday, October 31. On Friday, November 1, the first resolution was completed after four days of discussion. On Friday, November 1, the old age assistance resolution was completed as were the blindness allowance resolution, and in part the disabled persons allowance resolution. On Monday, November 4, the disabled persons resolution was completed. On November 4 also, second and third readings were given to the old age security bill. The others were given second and third readings on the Tuesday following.
The Secretary of State mentioned today that there was a timetable with regard to this matter. We appreciate this. We do not wish to hold up any measures affecting the elder citizens of Canada. But I would point out the number of days it took at that time to discuss the resolutions and the bills and I would remind him of the fact that the payments still were made to the people of Canada as of the 1st of November.
In 1962 we were faced with a somewhat similar position. On Monday, February 5, the old age security resolution was agreed to and the old age assistance resolution was discussed. On Tuesday, February 6, the old age security bill received second reading. On Wednesday, February 7, the old age security bill received third reading and the old age assistance resolution was passed, as was the blindness allowances resolution. On Thursday, February 8, the disabled persons allowances resolution was discussed and again on Friday, February 9. On Friday, February 9, second and third readings were given to the old age
Old Age Security
assistance bill and the blindness allowances bill while the disabled persons allowances bill received second reading only. It was postponed until Monday, February 12, at the behest of a member of the opposition of that day, at which time it was then given third reading.
This only points up that the plea of the Secretary of State today for fast passage of this legislation in order to try to help them out of a predicament into which they themselves walked is, I think, beyond comprehension. I should like to emphasize as strongly as I can that the increase now proposed would have been in the hands of our senior citizens by last August at the latest if the government had listened to the amendment proposed by the Leader of the Opposition on July 18. I should also like to emphasize that no ruling has yet been made on that amendment. I suggest that the government should accept it. Why not accept that amendment? If the government accepted it the same end would be achieved and our senior citizens would receive their just increase from that date. This party tried to get that increase through the house. The government has boobed again. It has bungled. It has procrastinated with the elder citizens. It is now playing politics with what should be rightfully theirs.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN AMOUNT OF PAYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we are very happy to have placed before us so soon after the reconvening of the session the resolution preceding the amending bill to increase the pensions of our senior citizens. There are many factors involved that require detailed study and analysis, but I do not think there is anyone who will disagree with the contention that this increase is past due. Our senior citizens have been waiting, I might say very patiently, for consideration of their needs. As I have indicated, we are very happy that we have this resolution before us at this time.
I feel there are a number of reasons why consideration must be given to the matter at this time. We are all aware of the fact that the cost of living is continuing to increase. This is placing our senior citizens, as well as others in the low income brackets, in a very difficult position. As they are endeavouring to face the increased cost of living and live on a decent standard, they are finding it almost impossible, if not impossible, on the present allowance of $65 per month.
I think there is another consideration, and it is this. Our senior citizens are observing a rising standard of living of a great many of their fellow Canadians. Although they recognize the assistance that has been given them in the past, yet they have a legitimate feeling that their income as well ought to be increased to take care of the situation and

Old Age Security
to help them enjoy some of the benefits that other citizens of Canada are enjoying now.
We have all had representations made to us concerning this particular matter. We have had letters from individual senior citizens or from senior citizens' organizations across the country pointing out the position in which these people find themselves now. Some of the provinces have recognized this need and are now providing supplementary benefits in order to assist our senior citizens in meeting the increased cost of living. In my own province of British Columbia, these people are receiving as much as $24 per month and this is of very real assistance in meeting the challenge before them today. May I say, Mr. Chairman, that not only our senior citizens but a great many people in other categories are facing similar problems. We hope that in the very near future the government will see fit to introduce legislation to assist these people who are facing serious economic conditions. I refer to the war veterans, the superannuated civil servants and different groups who are just barely getting by on pensions that were set some years ago.
It has been suggested that in the past this question has been made a political football, and unfortunately that has been so. Auction sale tactics have been used for political advantage in trying to gain the support of our senior citizens. I believe the time has come when we must take a sane and responsible attitude towards the necessity for making adequate provision for these people advanced in years. We are fully conscious of the fact that in a nation such as ours we are well able to provide adequately for those who, in building up this nation, have been unable to make provision for their declining years. I believe that today the responsibility is pressing, is urgent, and therefore we are very happy that this measure has been introduced at this time.
The method of financing, however, is open to question. We do not believe that an increase in taxation is necessary or desirable.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN AMOUNT OF PAYMENT
speechtext: How would you finance it?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN AMOUNT OF PAYMENT
speechtext:
We believe that the revenues coming into the federal treasury are sufficient if consideration were given to proper methods of financing and proper attention were given to monetary policies in relation to Canadian requirements. Therefore, while we would support without hesitation the proposal to increase this pension to $75, we would suggest that careful consideration be given to the matter of financing. If the government is convinced that additional taxation is required, then we would say that only sufficient additional revenue should be obtained or additional taxation levied to cover the actual cost

of administration in connection with this particular situation. Many times we find that instead of just sufficient revenue being collected to take care of additional expenditures, there is additional revenue required for something and this additional revenue is obtained under these various measures. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, we are not going to take any more time discussing this matter at the resolution stage. We are looking forward to the introduction of the measure, and various members of the group will be taking part in the discussion and making constructive criticism in relation thereto.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN AMOUNT OF PAYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, on behalf of this party I wish to indicate our pleasure that this proposal is before the house, namely to increase to $75 per month the pension paid under the Old Age Security Act. I should like also to indicate our pleasure that at least a beginning is being made in connection with this legislation on this first day that the house has met since the recess. I want to make it clear that I do not need a crying towel to assist me in expressing my pleasure that this proposal is now before the committee. I do not see any point in belabouring the fact that the government has changed its mind or gone through a flip-flop or what have you. The plain fact of the matter is that starting last July 18 opposition members in this house, and I think we were supported by the members on the government side as well, began to urge the government not to delay this $10 increase. We urged in every way we could that it be brought in at the earliest possible date.
Now the government has done this, and that is good. They have had a change of heart or whatever you may call it, and we welcome the fact that there is to be no further delay in making this increase in the pension paid under the Old Age Security Act. I hope we need not have any more time spent in berating the government for having done precisely what the house as a whole wanted it to do.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN AMOUNT OF PAYMENT
speechtext:
Perhaps if the hon. member gets an opportunity to speak in this debate he will explain that question, because the meaning of it escapes me completely.
I may say, Mr. Chairman, that we do wish the government would reconsider the effective date of this increase. The minister has indicated, and the resolution indicates also, that the effective date is to be October 1. This means, of course, that the $10 increase, if this legislation goes through in time, will be in

the cheques received by our old age security pensioners at the end of October. It is still our belief that this increase ought to be made retroactive at least to April of this year. I make that suggestion having in mind the fact that certain other increases that were provided in this chamber a short time ago were made retroactive to April, and indeed some other increases for civil servants and so on, were made retroactive to last October. I think the least we can do for our old age pensioners is to make this $10 increase retroactive to April of this year. I hope that somewhere along the line, while this legislation is before us, the government will consider making this change in the proposal that has been presented.
We agree that if we are going to ask and receive an increase in old age pensions we have to face up to the matter of paying for it, but we are puzzled as to why the government has proposed an increase in personal income tax of a full percentage point and has not made any suggestion about increasing the corporation tax. We also wonder if consideration has not been given to raising the ceiling on the amount that is paid under the Income Tax Act so far as old age security is concerned. We feel the rate might well have been left at 3 per cent, that the $90 ceiling could have been raised, and a percentage point added to the corporation tax. A method of that sort would be a fairer way of raising the money, rather than imposing a straight percentage point across the board on income tax.
We should have more details about this matter. Perhaps the Minister of National Health and Welfare will give us these details as we go along; but even so, I do not want undue time to be taken up because my concern is that this piece of legislation be put through so that the pensions can be adjusted and so that our old people can get this increase as soon as possible.
The main change which I think should be made in the legislation now before us relates to the effective date, and we in this party believe it ought to be made retroactive to April of this year.
I would also point out that it is recognized by all of us that this is just one step that is being taken with respect to improving the position of our old age pensioners, and we recognize that this step is being taken because the government was persuaded to change its mind during the so-called summer recess. That is the reason it was not on the order paper. The hon. member for Perth knows that, and he does not have to make such fuss because it was not on the order paper. On the night of August 2 the government had no intention of proceeding with this increase.
Old Age Security
Motions for today's order paper had to be in that day; but the government changed its mind in the meantime and so it was not technically possible to have it on the order paper. Today, however, we gave unanimous consent to proceed with it, and having done so we should not complain about the resolution not being on the order paper.
The whole question of the eligible age for receiving old age pensions is one with which we must grapple and to which we must find an answer. We in this party feel that the pension, as of right, must be available at age 65. We would like to see the Old Age Security Act amended to provide that the pension payable under it be payable at age 65, but we are not going to hold up this measure for that purpose. In the meantime I would go so far as to say that we welcome the statement made by the minister to the effect that consideration will be given, when the Canada pension plan is brought before the house, enacting legislation making it possible for people to take their old age security pension at an earlier age on a reduced basis.
Instead of our talking about 70 being the normal age, it should be the other way around. The normal age for people getting a pension as of right should be 65, and if people want to continue working past that age they should have the right to do so. Also if they want to delay taking their pension they should be able to receive a greater amount at a later age.
One of the real gaps in our present set-up is this five year period between the ages of 65 and 70. Retirement generally seems to be around 65 years of age. This is normal in industry and many other kinds of employment; but here the pension is put off until 70. During that five year period our people are in the wilderness and do not have what Canadians generally feel should be theirs as of right. Therefore I hope the consideration of this matter, which was implied in what the minister said this afternoon, will be speeded up as quickly as possible.
This leads me to say that I hope there will be the least possible delay in bringing forward the Canada pension plan in whatever revised form it will now have to be presented to us. Since the $10 increase in the old age security pension will no longer be an item in that plan, it seems to me this would involve a change in the computations, either a change in the amounts to be charged or a change in the amount of the pension. It will certainly call for a revision of that actuarial document which the minister provided a few days ago; and if one province is to stay out of the national plan, this too will call for certain changes in it. But, whatever changes are necessary, we urge the minister and the

Old Age Security
government to bring this matter before the house as soon as possible. Delay in placing before the house a proper pension plan, such as a joint arrangement of a flat rate pension and a contributory pension, could cost many years in providing the people of Canada with a desirable piece of social legislation.
In regard to this matter I want to make a plea directly to the minister. I urge her to get the chip off her shoulder as to where the opposition stands to a proper pension plan. She seems to think the opposition to adequate pensions lies with the other parties across the floor from her. She does not seem to know we want an adequate pension plan as much as she does. In fact there is more opposition to it from the people who are sitting behind her. By mistake I almost said the people sitting beside her, and maybe it was not a mistake after all.
I also suggest that she get the chip off her shoulder with regard to the province of Ontario. I am one of the last people in the house to defend the Tory government of Ontario, but I would say to the minister that a little wooing of the Ontario government in this field might be a little more effective than the sledge hammer tactics she has employed thus far. Indeed a little wooing of Quebec would be in order too.
The minister should realize that if there is opposition to this kind of pension plan, which she and the rest of us want, it does not come from those of us who are elected on a platform in favour of it. The opposition lies with the insurance companies, and she should realize she can get support from all sides of the house. In fact I think she can get support from the governments of Ontario and Quebec if she drops the political chip off her shoulder and if she realizes that, in the name of the people of Canada, all of us in this house should be working for a proper pension plan for all our people.
There has been talk about the timetable in getting this legislation through. By all means let us do it as quickly as we can, but it is also important to get the other legislation through at this session. If the kind of delays, which the Kilgours and some others are seeking, were permitted we would not get the Canada pension plan through this session, and if our outside opponents win it will be another session before we can have it. In the meantime a time will come when we will need another increase in the flat rate, and this will put off the day when we can get an old age security plan with both the flat rate and the contributory pension.
When we talk about pensions we are not talking about just enough money for people unable to provide for themselves in their old

age. We are talking about a social philosophy and real security for our older people.
We in this house are here as members of political parties. When we left on August 2 we were members of four political parties. Now we are members of five political parties. I do not expect, and in fact I would not want, politics to be removed from the House of Commons. Politics is the life of this house. It is out of the cut and thrust of debate and out of the cut and thrust of conflicting ideas that we are able to make progress. But if ever there was an area in which we should try to work together, I suggest it is in this field of providing adequate security for our older people.
The hon. member for Perth indulged in a little recent history. If he wants history we could tell him what happened 35 or 37 years ago when Mr. J. S. Woodsworth, the former member for Winnipeg North Centre, was here. We could speak of the early years of this century and recount the efforts made by trade unions to the governments of those days to get started on old age pensions. Having started, having the idea of pensions accepted, having the idea of universal pensions accepted, we now want adequate pensions provided, which can only be provided under the auspices of government and not private companies making their profit out of it. We have this principle accepted; let us work toward achieving this end.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare should make up her mind to seek our co-operation. She will get it from this side of the house. We congratulate her because she was not quite as political in her speech today as she usually is. I think she must have found it painful to make that moderate, objective statement. I see the minister nodding her head. This kind of pain is good for her, and if she will just stay with that kind of approach we will make good headway. I say again, Mr. Chairman, that we welcome this $10 increase and we are glad to be dealing with it on this first day of parliament following the recess. We hope this measure can be approved in very short order so that our people may receive this additional money in their cheques this month; and we hope the government will give consideration to making the date retroactive to last April.

Mr. Chairman, as has been said by each of the previous speakers, there is no question but that all hon. members of this house are in favour of the payment of an additional $10 a month to our senior citizens. I do not think anyone will take issue with that particular objective. But issue is taken, and rightfully so, with the methods used by the present government to bring about this increase.

Before entering into that particular phase of the matter I should like to say that in the hurried plan that has been put before us we are not told whether any consideration has been given to a differential payment. The method proposed, apparently, is following the same pattern that prevailed in the past, namely paying the same amount to everyone whether or not it is needed. I am not saying that is not the right way to do it, because I know it is extremely difficult to enter into a qualitative discussion or make a determination as to who should have more and who should not. It therefore becomes a question of raising enough money to pay everyone the $10 increase.
With regard to the question of the effective date of the commencement of this, it has already been said by one speaker, and I agree, that the date should be effective from April 8 last; the payment should be retroactive to that date. With regard to the period for raising the funds, I note that in the last paragraph of the statement which has been put into our hands there is a mention of a postponement in the collection of funds to meet this additional $10 payment, and it is to be applicable to 1964 and subsequent taxation years. In other words the Minister of National Health and Welfare and the present government intend to borrow money to meet this obligation, rather than raise it immediately out of taxes. They realize that if they wait until the 1964 income tax year, when we are filling out our income tax returns for that year it is quite possible we may have a different government, and they will leave on the door-step of that government the problem of raising this additional money in the form of taxes.

Mr. Chairman, I was most pleased to hear the hon. member for Macleod arguing just now for retroactive taxation in order to finance the increase in the old age security pension. This would not be acceptable to those on this side.
In the resolution which is before the committee the government, I believe, has taken a responsible position in saying that the proposed $10 increase in old age security must be financed by additional revenue. With the indulgence of the committee I should like briefly to outline the history of the old age security tax and the results of the government proposal to increase the contribution from personal income to the old age security fund in order to finance this well deserved increase in benefits to our senior citizens.
When the Old Age Security Act was passed in November, 1951 to provide pensions of $40 per month commencing January 1, 1952, the act provided for old age security taxes consisting of, first, a tax of 2 per cent on sales of goods subject to the general sales tax. This applied to all sales on and after January 1, 1952. Second, a tax of 2 per cent on the taxable income of corporations became effective January 1, 1952. Finally, a tax of 2 per cent on the taxable income of individuals, with a maximum tax of $60, was imposed. This tax was at the rate of 1 per cent, with a maximum of $30 for the 1952 taxation year.
In the budget of April 9, 1959 the then minister of finance announced that the old 2-2-2 formula of old age security taxes would be increased to a 3-3-3 formula. First of all the tax on sales was increased to 3 per cent with effect from April 10, 1959. Second, the tax on taxable income of corporations was increased to 3 per cent effective January 1, 1959. Finally, the tax on taxable income of individuals was increased to 3 per cent, with a maximum of $90, to take effect on July 1 1959.	'
Although the taxes imposed to raise revenues for the old age security fund had been referred to as the 2-2-2 formula, and more recently as the 3-3-3 formula, the amount derived from each of the three taxes has been far from equal.
The sales tax has provided by far the largest proportion, with the tax on individuals next and the tax on corporations producing the smallest portion. This I can illustrate in a table which, with the permission of the

Old Age Security
committee, I should like to have inserted in Hansard. May I have this permission, Mr. Chairman?

This table shows that for a single taxpayer who has an income of $1,500 per annum and takes the standard exemption, including the $100 exemption for donations, medical expenses and union dues, the old age security tax would increase his tax by $4 per annum, and the maximum contribution of $30 per annum would not be reached until he had an income of $4,100 per annum. So that the new tax would involve a maximum contribution of $30 per annum for a single person when that person reached an income level of $4,100. For married persons with no dependants, it would mean that there would be no contribution at a level of income of $2,000 per annum or less. At the level of $2,500 per annum the contribution required from individuals who are married and have no children is $4 per annum and the maximum contribution of $30 is not made by a married person until he reaches an income of $5,100 per annum. Similarly, if a person is married and has two dependants one would find that at an income level of $3,000 per annum his required contribution to the fund under the additional 1 per cent tax would only amount to $3, and the maximum contribution of such married person with two children amounting to $30 would not be reached until he earned $5,700.
The position of the old age security fund in recent years and up to March 31 of this year, the end of the last fiscal year, is shown on page 97 of the appendix to Hansard of June 13, in the budget papers. This indicates that at the end of last year there was a temporary loan from the Minister of Finance outstanding of some $41 million to make good the deficiency in the fund as of that time. The Minister of Finance stated that on the basis of the outlook and tax structure before the budget, the old age security fund would incur a further deficit of $25 million during the current fiscal year as reported on page
Old Age Security
1008 of Hansard at the bottom left hand side of the page. The removal of the exemptions from the sales tax were expected to add $45 million to the income of the fund in the current fiscal year, but this portion of the increase in the sales tax, payable into the old age security fund, was later deferred until 1965. The current expectation is that the taxes presently in effect, payable into the old age security fund, will yield $729 million this year, and the pensions before the increase of $10 that is being proposed will cost $750 million, leaving a deficit for the current fiscal year of $21 million. The $10 a month increase in the pensions will add $57 million to the amounts payable out of the fund, increasing the total to $807 million, and the increase of one per cent proposed in the contribution based on personal incomes will add $13 million to the revenues of the fund during the current fiscal year. This will leave the total fund with a deficit of some $65 million for the current year; that is, 1963-64.
It is expected that the additional 1 per cent contribution based on personal incomes which is proposed will yield approximately $100 million in a full fiscal year at current income levels. It is not feasible to put this increased contribution into effect forthwith, but only from January 1. For this reason the amount actually collected and credited to our accounts in the current fiscal year is relatively small. Nevertheless, the additional revenue being secured for the fund is roughly comparable with the additional $116 million being added to expenditures by the increase in the pension rate.
When one considers the situation in the next fiscal year it is of course less easy to make forecasts at this stage because of the greater difficulty of anticipating the levels of income at that time. Moreover, there will still be some lag in collections even in that year, owing to the delay in receipt of final payments of the taxes payable on 1964 incomes. For that year, therefore, we expect that this additional 1 per cent contribution will yield some $93 million that will compare with the additional cost of the $10 increase of approximately $116 million. On the other hand, we would anticipate some growth in the yield from the present taxes which would have produced a modest surplus of revenue over the pension payments during 1964-65. This increase in revenue would include a small amount from the application of the sales tax on building materials and machinery commencing in January, 1965. As a result, I would expect that the $93 million additional revenue which I have forecast from this additional 1 per cent contribution will, roughly, bring the old age security account into balance for the next fiscal year, that is, the 1964-65 fiscal

Old Age Security
year; the old age security fund, based on the increase of $10 which is being paid currently and the contributions from now to the end of the 1964-65 fiscal year will be brought into balance for that year.
Looking beyond that, I would expect there would be sufficient revenue available to make good relatively soon the deficit incurred in the current fiscal year. Thus, if the old age security payments were continued at $75 a month commencing at age 70 I would forecast some annual surplus in the fund each year beyond 1965. However, when the Canada pension plan is approved by parliament and benefits under the Old Age Security Act are paid at earlier ages, as is anticipated under the plan, the calculations which I have indicated will have to be adjusted accordingly.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, at the outset, it should be pointed out that we have no intention of delaying the present debate and that we cannot but be in favour of this increase in the pension for the aged in Canada or at least for those who have reached the age of 70 and who will receive it starting this month.
However, since there already exists a rather direct relationship with another pension scheme to be introduced later, I feel a few comments are in order concerning the two plans which are to be put forward this year.
First, we wish to ask the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss LaMarsh) to try and obtain the details of the new provincial contributory and portable pension plan for which a bill will be introduced at the next session of the Quebec legislature and to make them available to this house before the debate begins on this contributory and portable pension plan.
If a provincial government introduces a bill along that line, while the federal government introduces one also, the members of this house and those of the province concerned should be allowed to choose between the two pension plans.
It should not be believed that the electors in a province have necessarily made their minds up on that matter, Mr. Chairman. On the contrary, I believe that the citizens of the province of Quebec, as well as we in this house, must wait until they know all about those two schemes in order to be in a position to pick out that which will seem the most appropriate.
Of course, at first sight, we prefer the contributory and portable provincial pension plan because we want to protect the provincial autonomy which we respect. The leader of the government said last night on television, during a special program, that the provinces needed revenue to meet their increased responsibilities and that the same was true also for the federal government. Well, the responsibilities of the federal government have increased because it has taken over fields of jurisdiction that belonged to the provincial governments. Consequently, it would be fair to limit the responsibility of the federal government by handing over to the provincial governments the responsibilities and sources of revenue which are theirs under the British North America Act.
We tried to obtain details about the provincial portable and contributory pension plan,

but all we could gather from people close to the Quebec government is that apparently the province wants to set up a contributory and portable pension fund with accumulated funds. It is said that, over a period of four years, the accumulated funds would total $500 million. At that time, the government of the province of Quebec could use that half a billion dollars to develop certain sectors of the provincial economy. Otherwise, the provincial government would have to raise taxes or borrow elsewhere, from the chartered banks or the finance companies, or issue savings bonds. If the province of Quebec considers the establishment of a consolidated fund through the portable and contributory pension plan, it is precisely because it intends to borrow from that fund. In other words, it is using the pension scheme as an excuse to increase taxes. It also means that its contributory pension plan will be more costly and that a worker who contributes to a cumulative contributory pension plan will pay more than if he were contributing to a pension scheme under which there is no accumulation of funds.
If contributions are three times higher per month or per year than under the federal plan, he will have used it as an excuse to raise a new tax on personal incomes in the province of Quebec.
If the provincial government needs revenues through new taxes, it should say it without beating about the bush, instead of hiding the fact behind a new contributory and portable pension plan like the one which is now suggested. However, we will be able to make a decision only when those two plans are known and bills are introduced by the various governments.
That is why we feel that before introducing her bill or when introducing the legislation relating to the system of contributory and portable pensions, the minister of national health and social welfare should at least give us the opportunity to consider the bills which will be introduced by the government of the province of Quebec and by other provincial governments who will wish to establish their own pension plans, so that we can choose between them.
And now, Mr. Chairman-

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I had just finished expressing my views on the subject, but if I departed from the matter under discussion-I am sorry I did-it is because you had allowed some previous speakers to express their opinion on the contributory pension plan. I felt bound in my turn to inform the house of one of the reasons why the other act should be looked into most carefully.
As for the particular plan which is being submitted to us, that is the increase of old age pensions from $65 to $75, we are undoubtedly in favour of it and we shall see to it that it is passed as soon as possible.
However, in our opinion, the present government takes advantage of the situation to increase taxes, especially the additional 1 per cent tax on personal income tax. I agree with the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) who stated earlier that it would be difficult to increase further the sales tax, because it has just been increased in a very important field of our economy, i.e. in a field which accounts for $8.5 billion, namely building materials. Therefore, it was impossible to increase that 11 per cent sales tax.
But why should the burden of a tax increase such as this one, always be borne by the small wage earner? This burden is laid on the low income groups and again they will have to bear it.
Figures were quoted a while ago and I have noted a few which I should like to bring to the attention of the house.
For instance, we were told that in 1961, for the sole purpose of the old age security plan, personal income tax reached $229 million while corporation income tax amounted only to $103 million, which is less than half what is collected from individuals, from the small wage earners of our country.
Mr. Chairman, it was suggested a while ago that other sources of taxation could have been found. In my opinion, it would have been better for the population as a whole to raise the tax on corporation income.
Mr. Chairman, we know that in the United States, President Kennedy has come to the conclusion that taxes must be reduced in order to get the economy moving again. And I must confess that I was quite surprised to find that the present government had decided to increase taxes, because it is in the habit of following the Americans step by step and of doing everything they do.
Well, in order to rebuild the American economy, President Kennedy has reduced

Old Age Security
taxes by $11 billion in a single year. He expects that the annual income of each wage-earner will thus be raised by $340.
Right there and then, President Kennedy, with all his teams of economists and experts, says: that will enable us to rebuild our economy, to reduce unemployment and to encourage national production.
And what is being done in Canada? Exactly the opposite. An additional tax of 1 per cent is being levied on personal income.
Mr. Chairman, I submit that the Minister of National Health and Welfare could find another source of revenue, and it was precisely suggested to her by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) who, at that time, was replacing the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) who was absent.
In fact, we asked the Acting Minister of Finance if he could have borrowed from the Bank of Canada the $400 million he needed for loans to the municipalities. We asked him first if it was possible to do so, since the Liberal government had done it previously. The Minister of Trade and Commerce said then that it could be done but that it was not possible to borrow as much as $400 million.
Therefore, since the Minister of Trade and Commerce in the present government has stated that it could be done, I am of the opinion that the opportunity to do so is given him today and the amount is smaller now; it is expected to reach approximately $57 million the first year.
Mr. Chairman, if the ministers could agree among themselves, the Minister of National Health and Welfare might convince the Minister of Finance to adopt that proposal. Then I am convinced that the Minister of National Health and Welfare would become the first minister in any government to have increased the old age pension rate without increasing at the same time the income tax rate. To attain that distinction, she would have only to convince her colleague the Minister of Finance, since the Minister of Trade and Commerce is already convinced, that when a small amount is involved it is possible to get the money from the Bank of Canada.
Mr. Chairman, the Minister of National Health and Welfare seems to ask me where we should take the money without increasing taxes. Well, the Minister of Commerce himself made this suggestion, and as a reasonable amount is involved, that is an amount of $57 million, he suggests that we get it from the Bank of Canada. And as it is well known that the Canadian economy is in a state of stagnation, we would help to start it moving by so doing.
At the present time, we merely have money moving by taking it from wage earners to give

it to our citizens 70 years of age or over. But if we were getting the necessary money from the Bank of Canada, we would increase the purchasing power. We would not take money from the young people to give a little more to our old people. We would leave some to those who work and who have worked hard to earn their living and at the same time give a little more to our senior citizens.
Mr. Chairman, I will never be able to say how much we are against taxation, for taxation does not solve our problem; it only redistributes it as regards the citizens as a whole. On the other hand, we are in favour of the old age pensions' increase and that is the reason why we repeat our suggestion to the Minister of National Health and Welfare, for we believe that following the explanations given by the Minister of Trade and Commerce the other day, it would be possible for the ministers to agree to this suggestion for, after all, the amount involved here is a mere $57 million whereas the Liberal government of 1947 did not have any compunction to deal with $200 million.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to dwell for a moment on another question. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), has already raised that point a moment ago. Should we lower the age limit for old age pensions? We will naturally be told that, in so doing, we shall need new funds, and will thus have to increase the income tax. The present-day government seems to know of no other answer. However, let us think about the help we could bring to a great number of our fellow citizens, and boldly proceed with the proposed resolution.
A plant of the aluminum company is located in my own electoral district. Once they reach 65, the workers are pensioned off, and receive a monthly pension of $80 to $125 at the most. They are not entitled to anything else. For years, they have worked in the plant and at 65, as they can find no other work, particularly at a moment when unemployment is high, they have to wait five more years before receiving an old age pension which amounts to $75.
That, in my opinion, constitutes a gap which we should strive to fill and we should take steps so that those people who, at age 65, are used to a certain standard of living, should not have to work until they can get an extra $75 a month. Or perhaps, we should see to it that all those who are laid off or who are forced to retire because of a compulsory retirement plan or of an industry which no longer wants their services, people who have been unable to save any money because their salary was barely sufficient to make both ends meet, that such individuals

automatically benefit from a scheme under which they would get an old age pension of $75 per month at the age of 65.
The problem would be solved if a worker who is compelled to retire at the age of 65 because his services are no longer required, automatically received a pension of $75 a month even if he owns a house. But as it happens he is told today: you still own a house, sir, you still have a small bank account or something else in your name, a two-family dwelling, or something else. But if an individual has been clever or thrifty enough to buy a house, I do not see why, in order to be able to benefit from an old pension at 65 years, he should have to sell this house and wait for his capital to be spent before obtaining his $75 when he is 65. There is another suggestion I am making to the Minister of National Revenue. That any worker pensioned off at 65, should automatically come under the old age pension plan and get his pension from then on, so that there would be no more five-year period in his life during which he would not have enough to live decently or not be allowed to work.
Mr. Chairman, those are the few remarks I wanted to make on behalf of our group. I hope they will be favourably considered. They are not beyond the realm of possibilities. There is no exaggeration in these suggestions. The minister might have an estimate made of the additional cost to the pension fund so that those who are necessarily laid off benefit automatically from the old age plan without having to sell their house should they have one.
I believe that with all the tax increases that we have seen this year at the federal, provincial and municipal levels-the people are overburdened. And if that old age pension were to be financed through the Bank of Canada, I believe that the Canadian people would quickly forget about the vexations they have experienced and they would say; that minister managed to find the best way out of our economic problems in Canada.
