speechtext:
At the moment we have before us also the previous resolution embodying the proposal for a $10 increase in pension and the amendment moved by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition to make this $10 increase payable immediately. Certainly, the easiest method of implementing the government's desire would be to accept the amendment.
I was at a loss to understand the attaching of a monetary clause to this resolution by which taxes would be increased. Certainly the measure itself by which old age pensions are increased, compared to the contributory plan that the government previously considered, is broad enough in scope to allow us to debate both measures at one time. I suggest that the part of the measure by which taxes are increased would more properly be the subject of a separate budget resolution. I can understand why the government, in view of the trouble they have had with the budget and the number of changes they have had to make, would not be particularly anxious to introduce an individual budget item at this time. They hope, perhaps, that parliament and the country will treat them kindly in this respect because the old age pension item is attached to the item increasing taxes. Perhaps the two items are tied together because the government has finally become aware of just how much trouble they are running into in connection with their portable pension plan. They hope that this item, presented in this way, will draw attention away from that other pension plan and make the people of the country forget how much fire the government is drawing from various quarters in connection with that plan.
I realize, Mr. Chairman, that the specific resolution before us does not include the portable pension plan, but the method of financing is before us. We have to contrast this suggested method of financing with the method of financing suggested by this government just a couple of months ago in connection with the same item. I must say that the fact there were not even any copies of this resolution available until today makes me wonder if this measure was not brought before parliament in a great hurry. Certainly, it would not be the first time we have had reason to suspect this government of acting on impulse, not the first time we have seen them act hurriedly and without sufficient thought. Certainly the complete change from

Old Age Security
The previous plan suggested by the government is sufficient in itself to make us look with considerable suspicion on those wonders on the government benches who have made us wonder before.
If the change in content were not enough, certainly the change in the manner and method of presentation of the minister would be enough to make us wonder. Most of us who were present in the house when the hon. lady introduced the portable pension plan can recall the positive glee, the almost triumphant manner, in which she presented this plan. We can recall her saying with a beautiful smile, how glad she was to see pensions now being taken out of the realm of politics, while at the same time giving the most political speech ever given in the presentation of such a bill. Certainly this afternoon her speech was very short and her manner most subdued. In fact, the amount of information that she gave was minute. One gained the impression that the minister had learned from her previous dealings on the subject of pensions in this house, and the public and press reaction, that perhaps the less said by her-the better. It might be, too, that the result of her intervention in the Ontario provincial election, the reaction of her opponents as well as the reaction of the voters of this province, has taught her a lesson that perhaps will have a lasting effect not only on the hon. lady but on her conduct in this house.
I am in agreement with the increase in the old age pension, and I am sure most of us have realized the house must pass this needed piece of legislation. We all urge the government to honour the commitment it made to the voters during the last election to give this increase immediately. We recall how indignant we were when the government indicated it had no intention of carrying out that commitment and how it denied there was a commitment to put the increase into effect immediately.
I continue to be amazed at the manner in which the members of the government can use the English language. I am amazed at the lengths to which they will go to find a commitment on the subject of nuclear arms. Here we find the government committing itself to a policy it does not agree with, and stretching the English language as an excuse for doing so. On the other hand, and for a very worthy project on which they convinced every voter in the country they were committed to a $10 pension raise, they are unable to find a commitment, and have been unwilling to honour it until forced into doing so by the events and public pressure of the last few months.
I am sure most of us who know Canada's prosperity as a nation and the general standard

of living we enjoy, realize that this makes it mandatory on us to recognize our responsibility to our old people in a substantial form. This $10 increase is justified and it is incumbent on us to pay it. In saying that, I am not unmindful of our responsibility to raise the money and to consider how it will be raised. However I am a little surprised to find this subject tied in at the same time as the increase is being passed.
It is not usual in the House of Commons, whenever a bill is presented calling for an expenditure of funds, to tack on to it a clause in the resolution preceding it outlining in detail the method by which the money should be raised. In fact the customary procedure is to deal with the matter in two stages, to consider whether we ought to carry out certain plans and then at another time consider the question of raising money for that purpose in the debate on raising money generally. In this manner we are able to keep our spending and the raising of money in proportion and each item, taken together with all the rest, is capable of being assessed regarding its effect on the tax paying ability of the country.
Dealing with the present measure, we have to consider not only whether the old age pension should be increased but we have also to decide whether we should change the general formula which has existed for the last 10 or 12 years, of finding increased funds for pension purposes by an orderly increase on each of three classes of taxpayers. We have to consider whether it is wise for the house to vary that formula, and I submit that this question alone could be the subject of a very long and learned debate.
It is worthy of note that the minister made only passing reference to the subject of raising the money. It was only after three or four hon. members had spoken on the subject that the parliamentary secretary contributed to the debate and we heard any discussion on the question of raising the necessary funds. Considering that the subject of taxation is rather difficult at the best of times, and knowing you cannot raise taxes in one area without having a considerable influence on the wellbeing of the general economy of the country, I would think the government would have been anxious to approach this subject of additional taxation with some diffidence, and to have approached the subject of a change in the concept of taxation with some difference, and furthermore with some advance notice.
We were told a couple of weeks ago that the government planned to increase old age pensions, but I do not think we were told exactly how it was to be done. There was nothing on the order paper and nothing was

said specifically about it until today. I suggest that this is rather a quick method of asking the house to deal with so serious a subject. In fact I begin to wonder whether the minister has really learned to leave politics out of these questions.
It looks to me like another political trick to propose the increase and the financing of it in such a way that we, as legislators, would be rather careless in looking at it and examining it closely. Then, if we dare to examine or question the propriety and wisdom of raising the money in this manner, it could be said we were guilty of prolonging debate and keeping the old age pensioners from getting their money. However I believe that the people of the country will see through this political trick.
I suggest the minister has not learned that public pressure is not just brought about by insurance companies complaining about portable pension plans. Public pressure is the awareness of the ordinary men and women of Canada of what is going on. It is the realization by them that the Liberal government came into power because of what it promised to do, and this is a commitment the government had to carry out because of that public pressure. Even at this late date I would suggest the government would be well advised to accept the amendment moved by the Leader of the Opposition.
I have a few questions in my mind despite the illuminating and interesting information supplied by the parliamentary secretary. There are the questions of other expenses that usually accompany a straight raise in old age pensions. Contributory pensions usually go up at the same time, and there are the same considerations to be given to contributory widows pensions and blind pensions. We will run into all these increases. The argument that holds good for one holds good for the others. They usually have gone up at the same time, so that added to the question of whether the government has acted properly in tying in this method of raising money with the increase in pensions, is the question of whether it has only attacked the problem piecemeal.
Surely public pressure on the Liberal government which forced them to agree to this $10 increase is not to be satisfied by this sort of action without regard to the kind of common sense it makes. The same public pressure will want to know about the other pensions; it will want to know why the government has not handled them all together, and it will want to know why the government does not put its taxation house in order all at once. Certainly the fact is that so little is left of the budget, and the ordinary citizen of Canada
Old Age Security
is so much in doubt as to where the finances of this country are, that a new budget for this year is more than past due.
Mr. Chairman, I would suggest that instead of putting these two things, the money spending and the money raising, in the same resolution, the government should merely put through the old age pension increase and the minister should tell us what she intends to do about the contributory pensions, pensions for the blind, etc. Then the government can put its mind to work on the question of bringing in a new budget. The parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance quoted some figures which indicate-if I sorted it out in my mind correctly, and without the tables to which he referred it was rather difficult to get them straight; but I made some notes -that the 1 per cent increase in the old age security tax payable by the individual would amount to about $90 million in a taxation year. When the minister made her statement to the house she said the difference in cost on this one item would amount to about $116 million for a year. So that for the one year the two items are nearly ad idem and it would seem, whether I use the term "taxation year", "fiscal year" or "calendar year", this will not be too inaccurate. I do not want to get confused, as did my hon. friend from Macleod, with regard to what we call the year. I take it that whatever year we are talking about, it is the same year, calendar or taxation.
However, I remember the minister's speech on the contributory plan and I note that we still have this on the order paper, and we have had no indication from the government that it intends to drop the contributory plan. We are going to have the complication of financing that, which may have a bearing on the amount of money realized from this increase in taxation and which is certainly going to have an influence on the ability of the taxpayer to pay it. I am wondering whether the minister, when she next deals with this topic, would mind straightening out the house in this regard, bearing in mind some of her remarks of July 18 as reported in Hansard, where she made reference to the variable amounts that might be required to be paid out under the contributory scheme.
All we know about the participation of the other provinces in the federal scheme is that apparently Quebec is not going to take part in it. I would think that in itself might be warning enough to the minister that some of the weighted criticism across the country with regard to the portable pension scheme is perhaps worth looking at very closely.
We are not sure, of course, that the rest of the provinces are going to agree, and perhaps of more moment to this debate is the fact

Old Age Security
that the provinces may very well ask the minister to reconsider part of that other scheme. That part may be the method of financing and the amount of contributions, etc. We certainly saw, for instance, in the winter works program that the government had to practically throw out its scheme and adopt the one the provinces wanted, in order for them to accept it. We do not have the acceptance of the provinces and I therefore suggest it is quite possible that the provinces may force the government to bury its contributory scheme to the extent that the fund raising aspects of it will throw a totally new and unexpected load on the government.
I suggest that even though, as the minister said originally with regard to the contributory scheme, we are not exactly fixed on the contributions from the individual, that part of the finances the provinces expect the federal government to pay will have to come from additional sources of tax revenue. It might very well be that the minister will be in the position of having to come back to the house and say, "I want to increase each of the categories from 3 per cent to 4 per cent"; that is, not just the tax on the individual, but the sales tax and the corporation tax, right across the board. In that case we would be presented with a whole new set of figures.
Might I suggest to the minister that she seriously consider withdrawing from this resolution the fund raising part of it. Also, I suggest that an entirely new budget be presented, or an amendment to the budget, so that we can get on with granting the increase in pension without this further complication, and so we can give the fund raising aspect of this matter the kind of attention it deserves.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN AMOUNT OF PAYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, during the last federal election, the hon. Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss LaMarsh) was a member of the truth squad. Probably worried about her conversion, she remembered the words of Socrates, the philosopher: Know thyself. Then, she changed her mind but she nevertheless retained a certain personal knowledge which she has used today and which she acquired while she was following the present Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) who was Prime Minister at the time. The best evidence we have of that is the resolution which the minister introduced this afternoon. Indeed, the hon. lady had to agree that the Leader of the Opposition spoke the truth last July 18 when, seconded by the hon. member for Perth (Mr. Monteith), he moved the following amendment:
That the said resolution be amended by adding after the words "ten dollars a month" in line 9:

"and this house asks that the government give consideration to making the payment of such additional pension to commence on this day."
The Minister of National Health and Welfare has now decided to accept this proposed amendment. At that time, she and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chevrier) rose and stated emphatically that the proposed amendment was unconstitutional. And I think it is you, Mr. Chairman, who on that day said that you would take under advisement the matter of legality of the amendment proposed by the Leader of the Opposition. In my opinion, the resolution introduced this afternoon by the minister relieves you from rendering a decision which we were anxious to know.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare accepts the suggestion made by the Leader of the Opposition, except for the last words of the amendment: "to commence on this day", because the resolution before us indicates that this legislation on old age security will come into force on October 1, 1963.
I would like, Mr. Chairman, to draw your attention to a particular point which came up in discussing this resolution. I did not look very deeply into the matter, but I wonder if the resolution does not come in conflict with some clauses or rules of the house, because I do not know whether we are allowed two resolutions on one bill. I shall not stress the point, I only mention the fact. But, I wonder if it is not creating more of that confusion often found among government members, and which is characteristic of them since they took over. If we look over the text of the resolution introduced this afternoon, and refer to number 15 on the order paper, we shall see that it also mentions an increase of $10 a month in the pension paid under the Old Age Security Act.
No doubt the leader of the house, the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pick-ersgill) did not have time to submit the question to the government's legal adviser because after the triduum which followed the closed retreat of last week end which the members of the Liberal party attended, I think the Minister of National Health and Welfare-in order to regain political prestige was forced to submit this resolution in a hurry, without studying all its legal aspects. But there is no doubt that all members of the house will support this motion since we of the official opposition, were in favour of a $10 per month increase as early as July 18, we still are, even more than ever.
That legislation, as I said a moment ago, was prepared in great haste, did not have time to ripen or to be completed, and could

not give satisfaction to all those who need social aid in any guise or form from the federal government.
Besides, the Minister of National Health and Welfare when she saw at the last federal-provincial conference that her contributory pension scheme was turning out to be a failure-a failure that was much more humiliating since it was coming on the heels of the last federal election-then, the minister should have taken the opportunity offered her when she met with the provincial premiers to discuss the advisability of amending the act in order that the provinces and the federal government might offer pensions not only to those over 70 years of age, but also to those now coming under the handicapped and blind persons acts.
Now, I believe that the minister of health and welfare, as well as the government, would have shown the Canadian people that their plan was not submitted for the purpose of bolstering the Liberal party which is sinking fast since it is the first constructive piece of legislation introduced by this government.
Since April we have been faced only with incomplete legislation meant to put the taxpayer in a difficult position. I am thinking of those different taxes which have been levied by a certain minister of finance who turns out to be a pretty poor administrator. He may be a competent accountant, but as far as I am concerned, he does not know the first thing about administration. Besides, the measure brought forward is nothing but patchwork and intended to make the people forget the government's mismanagement at this time and, as the previous speaker just said, I think that the government should not introduce immediately this legislation to impose a 4 per cent tax to provide for the increase of that pension. We should rather be given the opportunity to think over and revise the whole social legislation. Then, the government might find out in that financing method a form of taxation which would not only help to meet the expenses of its social assistance plan, but also help all the various classes of society, the various classes of government pensioners.
I think the minister should give more thought to the old age problem even though the government will not get much political advantage from it. When the Prime Minister made his announcement during the last election campaign in Ontario, several old persons in my riding were delighted over the statement, but everyone without any exception told me that the Prime Minister was afraid of being defeated in the house and that it is the Leader of the Opposition who imposes his views and makes the government realize
Business of the House
that to keep that election pledge is in their own interest.
Last year, when we introduced legislation to raise from $55 to $65 the payments to all government pensioners, there was no mention of new taxes to be imposed. It is to be hoped that the famous planning program will be carried out without new taxes having to be imposed on Canadian taxpayers.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I should like to ask the house leader if he would give us a forecast of the business for the rest of the week, which I hope will be done in orderly fashion without these special requests to go on after the hour, and things of that nature.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think most hon. members will feel that the country will expect us, even if we once in a while have to sit a little late, to do the country's business.
The first item we shall take tomorrow is the continuation of this debate, and if it is completed, as I hope it will be, we shall then take the two bills respecting Northwest Territories. I may say there is some urgency about these because of the need to hold an election in the territories this autumn. If they are completed there is a resolution standing in the name of my colleague the Minister of Labour with respect to vocational training which would be taken next.
If we conclude the debate on the old age pension resolution we would want to take the bill on Wednesday, and on Thursday, I should like to suggest, the Minister of Finance will be asking for interim supply. It was our thought that we would ask for two months

Business of the House
supply so as not to interrupt our business again. We would hope in that time to be able to get through all the estimates.
The resolution respecting the measure to which the Minister of Labour referred earlier today will appear on the notice paper of today and will, of course, appear on the order paper on Wednesday. We would expect to advance it one stage on that day. As the minister has indicated, its progress beyond that stage will depend to some extent on developments which may or may not take place outside the house. It is therefore necessary to have some reservations about business in the latter part of the week.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: May I ask the leader of the house a question? If, as we hope, the debate on the old age pension resolution is ended early tomorrow, might it not be possible to have the bill printed and proceeded with later tomorrow in place of some of the other legislation to which the hon. gentleman has referred?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That would be exceedingly agreeable to the government, but unanimous consent would be required.
It being five minutes after ten o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Tuesday, October 1, 1963
